title: OpenGray: a benchmark for evaluating the decisions of radiotherapy planning agents
abstract: arXiv:2610.37081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background and purpose: Radiotherapy planning agents based on large language models (LLMs) decide when to submit a plan or request review but are evaluated mainly by dose. This study developed OpenGray, a benchmark of planning tasks with known correct decisions. Materials and methods: OpenGray adds tasks with known answers to the OpenKBP-Opt head-and-neck dataset, including two contradictions with dose goals proven incompatible and a feasible control with a stored plan meeting every hard goal. Four systems, from a rule-based planning script to a full LLM agent, were evaluated on 30 patients, the LLM-based ones with a commercial (Terra) and a local (Ministral 3 8B) LLM. Decisions, achieved dose, problem recognition, and technical failures were recorded and also read from logs of 39 stereotactic radiosurgery runs of SAGE, a clinical LLM agent. Results: With Terra, the script preceded by an LLM review and the full agent had decision accuracies of 95.4% and 92.1%, respectively, yet escalated only 50% (95% confidence interval, 25-75%) and 25% (10-40%) of overlap contradictions, which required arithmetic on the anatomy. All four systems submitted every feasible control, but 24% of these plans missed a hard goal that the stored plan had met. In four SAGE runs, one goal failed at every attempt; the agent identified it in every reply but had no action for stopping. Conclusions: Favorable aggregate scores concealed specific decision failures. Planning agents should be evaluated on their decisions as well as their dose and given an explicit action for stopping and requesting review.

title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
abstract: arXiv:2610.37571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team's success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss. Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.

title: State of clinical AI in 2026
abstract: Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced rapidly, with frontier large language models now matching or exceeding physician performance on simulated diagnostic reasoning and clinical decision-support tasks. Yet adoption has outpaced the evidence base: fewer than 5% of cleared U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) AI/machine learning (ML) devices have undergone peer-reviewed evaluation and prospective randomised trials remain scarce. This narrative review synthesises evidence from ARISE’s State of Clinical AI Report 2026 across six domains: model performance and human benchmarking, evaluation methodology and benchmark validity, foundational methods including multimodal and multiagent systems, clinical workflow integration, patient-facing applications and applied domain-specific AI. We conducted a targeted literature search of PubMed, medRxiv and arXiv supplemented by expert nomination, including empirical studies of AI in clinical contexts. Across domains, frontier models demonstrate strong clinical reasoning capabilities but exhibit persistent failures in uncertainty calibration, metacognition and robustness to distributional shift. Standard benchmarks have saturated, prompting development of multidimensional evaluation frameworks that assess safety, real-world workflows and agentic capabilities. New trends in foundational methods include converting medical data into tokens and developing multiagent, multimodal systems. In clinical workflows, early prospective trials in clinical decision support and diagnostic imaging show promising results, though human-AI collaboration remains suboptimal and risks of automation bias and clinician deskilling are emerging. In tandem, patient-facing AI is progressing with more personalised health assistance; with this comes the risk of patient overtrust, raising the bar for guardrails. The most credible translational progress occurs on narrowly defined tasks with clear endpoints, while broader clinical autonomy awaits advances in evaluation and human-AI interaction.

title: Keeping clinical evidence current as medical artificial intelligence systems change
abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence systems may change faster than clinical evidence can be generated, reviewed, and implemented. Updates to the foundation model, prompt, retrieval layer, generation settings, tools, memory, interface, or workflow can alter behaviour without changing the product name visible to investigators or users. This Perspective synthesizes evidence on repeated-run instability, cross-version performance, human–AI interaction, agentic systems, and post-deployment monitoring. We propose VERSION-AI as a testable evidence-refresh framework that separates what changed from the clinical consequences of failure. C0–C8 describe the system or context change, whereas a distinct clinical-consequence tier reflects intended use, decision dependence, time sensitivity, and the likelihood and severity of harm from incorrect, omitted, or delayed actions. The combination determines whether evidence may remain current after audit, requires usability or repeated-run bridging, cross-version or local validation, shadow evaluation, continuous monitoring, rollback capability, or renewed prospective clinical assessment. Because VERSION-AI has not yet been prospectively validated, it is presented as a research and governance proposal rather than a regulatory instrument. Evidence transfer after a material system change should be demonstrated rather than assumed.

title: Development and Pilot Evaluation of a Standardized and Accessible Rubric (OMNI) for Assessing Generative AI in Health Care Contexts: Four-Stage Mixed Methods Study
abstract: Background: The rapid adoption of generative AI in the community and health care necessitates reliable, human-led evaluation. Objective: This study aimed to develop a standardized rubric to support health care professionals, administrators, and researchers in evaluating generative AI outputs in health contexts. Methods: A rubric was developed through a 4-stage mixed methods study: literature synthesis, expert refinement, pilot application, and post-pilot feedback. The rubric was informed by 69 publications and refined through iterative feedback from a multidisciplinary expert panel (n=23). The pilot rubric was applied to 4 health care scenarios: responses to health-related Reddit questions, generation of health-related images and videos, responses to health professional continuing education questions, and automated physician-to-physician clinical documentation generation. Via these scenarios, 15 clinicians (medical practitioners, pharmacists, and medical oncologists) evaluated 250 input-output pairs using domain-level ratings and qualitative comments. The evaluated outputs included 200 AI-generated responses across the 4 health care scenarios and 50 physician-tagged replies in the health-related Reddit questions scenario. Results: The final rubric, OMNI, comprised 10 evaluation domains (Accuracy, Safety, Recognizes Uncertainty, Completeness, Communicates Clearly, Empathetic, Context Aware, Referencing, Follows Instructions, and Avoids Coerciveness) assessed on 4-point Likert scales, supported by detailed instructional and example materials. Via the 4 pilot scenarios, assessors generated 9600 domain-level ratings and 4010 qualitative comments. The mean pairwise agreement for the 4-point Likert groups ranged from 30.8% to 53.4%, increasing to 59.3% to 79.6% when collapsed into broad agreement categories; Gwet’s AC2 ranged from 0.49 to 0.80. OMNI differentiated strengths and weaknesses between models within scenarios, while recurrent limitations in Referencing, Recognizes Uncertainty, Completeness, Empathetic, and Accuracy were identified across scenarios. Multimodal image and video outputs had the highest occurrence of negative rating domains. Assessors reported OMNI was usable and indicated they would reuse it. Conclusions: OMNI is a standardized, accessible rubric for expert-led evaluation of generative AI outputs in health contexts. Pilot application demonstrated that OMNI could differentiate AI performance across models and domains while generating structured feedback. Further work is needed to assess its applicability to purpose-built health AI tools, agentic systems, and organizational evaluation settings.

title: MedSegAgent: A Universal and Scalable Multi-Agent System for Instructive Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Medical image segmentation is vital for clinical diagnosis and treatment; however, current solutions face three major limitations: (1) the lack of a universal framework capable of handling diverse modalities and anatomical targets, (2) the limited scalability to adapt to evolving clinical needs and new datasets, and (3) the lack of instructive interfaces that make models usable for non-expert users. To address these challenges, this paper presents MedSegAgent, a universal and scalable multi-agent system for instructive medical image segmentation. Specifically, MedSegAgent comprises five agents: one query parsing agent that processes natural language requests, three coarse-to-fine filtering agents (modality filtering, anatomical filtering, and label selection) for identifying relevant datasets and label values, and one execution agent responsible for model inference and result integration. Based on this framework, MedSegAgent utilizes 23 diverse datasets and pre-trained models to perform 343 types of segmentation across various modalities and anatomical targets. Experimental results demonstrate that MedSegAgent simplifies model selection while maintaining high performance, accurately identifying matching datasets and labels in 94.27% of queries and locating at least one suitable match in 99.03% of queries. MedSegAgent offers a universal and scalable solution for diverse medical image segmentation tasks, bridging the gap between user-friendly queries and the complexities of model selection and deployment.

title: Using a large language model artificial intelligence agent to improve the efficiency of clinical quality measure evidence evaluation: a case study
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the feasibility and performance of a large language model (LLM)-based artificial intelligence (AI) agent, implemented within a structured Claim–Argument–Evidence System (CAES), for supporting the review of clinical quality measure (CQM) evidence in the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Consensus-Based Entity (CBE) endorsement process. Methods The CBE conducted a pilot study using a previously endorsed measure. CAES extracted claims and citations from a submitted diagnostic performance measure for pneumonia, automatically retrieved additional relevant evidence from PubMed abstracts and assessed the quality, confidence and agreement of evidence supporting each claim. The system’s assessments were compared with the judgement of a subject matter expert (SME). Results CAES completed the assessment in approximately 5 hours. The SME agreed with the CAES-assigned claim statuses for 69% of claims, was neutral for 11% and disagreed for 14%. Disagreements primarily stemmed from the need for contextual interpretation beyond abstracts. Discussion Manual evaluation of CQM evidence requires significant time and resources, estimated at over 2400 labour hours per review cycle, limiting efficiency and transparency. The AI agent evaluated 64 claims and 355 claim–evidence pairs related to the pneumonia diagnosis measure. It assigned claim statuses based on evidence strength and generated justifications. Conclusion This pilot demonstrated the feasibility and potential of LLM-based AI agents to improve the efficiency and transparency of evidence review for CQMs. Further development is needed to incorporate additional data sources and extend applicability across the measure development lifecycle.

title: Development and Validation of Human-AI Collaborative Workflow in SNOMED CT Mapping of Bilingual Clinical Text
abstract: Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine–Clinical Terminology (SNOMED CT) is the principal international standard for semantic interoperability of clinical information, but mapping free-text clinical narratives to SNOMED CT concepts remains labor-intensive. We developed a large language model agent system for mapping bilingual clinical text to SNOMED CT concepts and evaluated its effect on mapping accuracy and efficiency within a human-AI collaborative workflow. We designed a three-module agent system comprising translation, abbreviation expansion, and vector-based retrieval components, integrated with a pre-embedded SNOMED CT vector database. Three health information managers independently mapped bilingual clinical text segments using three approaches: human-only, Agent-only, and Agent-assisted human mapping. title: Audiologist-Guided Multimodal AI for Pure-Tone Audiometry and Tympanometry Interpretation and Reporting
abstract: Multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) could support audiology reporting, but an end-to-end score can obscure whether errors arise from image transcription, specialty-rule execution, or communication. We evaluated these as separate modules in 155 de-identified outpatient records representing 151 patients. In Module 1, schema-only and audiologist-skill prompts were compared in 50 development records; the locked skill was then tested with a Codex GPT5.5 agentic workflow in 101 independent patients. A post hoc robustness analysis tested matched schema-only and skill-assisted direct-API conditions with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp in the same 101 patients. The skill increased hearing-loss-type agreement from 85.0% to 94.0% and acoustic-reflex agreement from 70.4% to 98.4% in development. Codex validation yielded 1809/1820 (99.4%) exact numeric thresholds, but only 9/15 (60.0%) no-response entries were correct. In the DeepSeek robustness analysis, the skill increased type agreement from 37.6% to 70.3%, while exact numeric-threshold agreement remained 72.1% and no-response agreement remained 0%. In Module 2, AI workflows received adjudicated structured values, not Module 1 outputs. After two audiologists refined reports using 60 records, 91 independent patients were evaluated. All 25 rule-derived fields were correct in 91/91 Codex and 87/91 DeepSeek cases; both audiologists rated all Chinese reports accurate or basically accurate. These were different operational workflows, not a matched foundation-model comparison. The findings support prospective evaluation of modular, auditable clinician assistance, not autonomous diagnosis, end-to-end performance, or patient usability.

title: MR-MAS: an end-to-end multi-agent system for autonomous Mendelian randomization analysis
abstract: Abstract Motivation Understanding disease-related causal mechanisms is essential for biomedical research, yet the practical use of Mendelian Randomization (MR) remains constrained by fragmented analytical workflows and a strong dependence on specialized expertise. These challenges limit the efficient, standardized, and reproducible execution of end-to-end MR analyses. Results We propose MR-MAS, an end-to-end automated MR analysis system built on a multi-agent architecture. MR-MAS leverages the reasoning and coordination capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and integrates external tools to unify data acquisition, causal effect estimation, results interpretation, and manuscript preparation into a single workflow, thereby reducing manual effort. MR-MAS further incorporates a structured Mendelian Randomization Knowledge Base (MRKB) to support MR method implementation and targeted repair of MR analysis code. Across diverse test scenarios, MR-MAS demonstrated stable workflow execution, reproduced several literature-supported causal signals, and maintained consistent causal estimates across repeated runs and different model backends. Additional evaluations showed robust trait retrieval and improved code-repair performance with MRKB guidance. These results suggest that MR-MAS may provide practical support for scalable, standardized, and reproducible MR analyses in biomedical research. Availability and Implementation The source code, MRKB, and benchmark data are freely available at https://github.com/Zaiwen/MR-MAS , with the version used in this study archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20342636 .

title: CohortFlow: A Steerable Clinical Cohort Curation Agent with Localized Semantic Correction
abstract: arXiv:2610.36100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model agents for clinical cohort curation should accommodate evolving eligibility criteria without repeatedly processing unchanged requirements. We introduce CohortFlow, a steerable agent that represents natural language corrections as localized updates to a structured cohort specification and reconciles them with a persistent execution graph. Explicitly recorded semantic dependencies enable affected computations to be selectively invalidated while preserving valid prior results. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria, comprising 126 correction turns, localized steering achieves 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B model, a small numerical advantage that is not statistically significant ($p=0.493$). It reduces mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept evaluation over MIMIC, all 13 cohort states execute successfully, while correction trajectories demonstrate selective preservation of unaffected computations and recomputation of changed or dependent nodes. Together, these results show that localized semantic steering can substantially reduce correction latency and model calls while maintaining strong requirement-level accuracy.

title: Changes in the acceptance of artificial intelligence in medicine among physicians and the general public in Japan: A repeated cross-sectional comparison of 2018 and 2025
abstract: by Teppei Suzuki, Honoka Tamori, Kazuki Ohashi, Yasuhiro Morii, Kenji Hirata, Kohsuke Kudo, Katsuhiko Ogasawara Medical artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced rapidly, yet whether growing societal familiarity with AI is accompanied by greater willingness to receive relatively autonomous AI-led care remains unclear. We conducted repeated cross-sectional online surveys in Japan in 2018 and 2025 using the same questionnaire and compared self-identified physicians and members of the general public (2018: 399 physicians and 600 members of the public; 2025: 300 physicians and 300 members of the public). Mean responses to the item assessing intention to use medical AI did not differ significantly between survey years in either group, despite consistently favorable evaluations of its usefulness and future necessity. Among physicians, the unadjusted mean response regarding the potential of medical AI to improve clinical efficiency was higher in 2025, but this difference was not significant after adjustment for age and sex. Among members of the public, self-rated knowledge of medical AI was higher in 2025, while expectations that medical AI would increase healthcare costs were also greater. These findings suggest that increased self-rated knowledge may not necessarily be accompanied by greater intention to use relatively autonomous medical AI. Implementation strategies should therefore address concerns regarding responsibility, safety, data protection, and healthcare costs alongside efforts to improve public understanding.

title: Causes of mortality in humanitarian crises requiring coordinated response: a scoping review protocol
abstract: Introduction Mortality patterns in humanitarian crises are shaped by intersecting factors including violence, displacement, health system disruption and environmental shocks. While crude and under-five mortality rates are often tracked, less is known about specific causes of death across diverse crisis contexts. Existing guidance informing humanitarian response is largely informed by outdated evidence and does not account for demographic, epidemiological and geopolitical shifts over the past two decades. This review aims to synthesise available data on cause-specific mortality in humanitarian settings to inform improved monitoring, policy and response. Methods and analysis We will conduct a scoping review of peer-reviewed and grey literature reporting on causes of death in humanitarian crises between 2015 and 2025. Eligible studies will include crisis-affected populations in locations with an active Humanitarian Response Plan during analysis. We will search Medline, Embase and Global Health, and screen organisational datasets from key humanitarian agencies. A large language model will be used to assist with title and abstract screening. Full-text screening and data extraction will be conducted manually by two reviewers. Methodological quality will be assessed using study-type-specific appraisal tools. Data will be extracted using a standardised plan and synthesised narratively. Ethics and dissemination Ethics approval is not required as this study uses publicly available data. Findings will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal and disseminated via policy briefs, academic presentations and targeted stakeholder engagement.

title: Public health surveillance systems involving Indigenous Peoples: a scoping review protocol to inform circumpolar mental health and wellness surveillance
abstract: Introduction Mental health and well-being are urgent priorities across circumpolar regions, where suicide and psychological distress contribute substantially to premature mortality and disability. Indigenous communities in Arctic and sub-Arctic settings continue to face profound inequities linked to colonisation and intergenerational trauma, while also advancing wellness frameworks grounded in cultural continuity, language, land and self-determination. Progress in mental health promotion and suicide prevention depends on timely, consistent and culturally relevant population-level information. Yet mental health surveillance remains fragmented, and the literature has not been comprehensively mapped to describe how public health surveillance systems are designed, governed, implemented and used in Indigenous contexts. This review aims to inform culturally grounded mental health and wellness surveillance in circumpolar Indigenous contexts. This will be achieved by mapping how public health surveillance systems involving Indigenous Peoples are designed, governed, implemented and used, and identifying transferable lessons for circumpolar monitoring. Methods and analysis This scoping review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews and will be reported using Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. Using a Population–Concept–Context framework, we will include peer-reviewed and grey literature published in the past 20 years (English and Scandinavian languages) describing public health surveillance systems implemented with, by or for Indigenous communities. This will cover the period of January 2006 to August 2026. Mental health, suicide, substance use and wellness-related systems will be prioritised. Searches will be conducted in MEDLINE, Embase and APA PsycInfo, complemented by targeted grey literature searching of relevant organisational and government sources. A health sciences librarian will execute all database searches and export results for screening. One reviewer will conduct the grey literature searches, documenting search dates, sources and retrieval decisions. Two reviewers will independently screen all records retrieved and extract data using a structured charting tool capturing system characteristics, governance and data stewardship, ethics, implementation considerations, uses of surveillance information and circumpolar relevance. Findings will be summarised descriptively and synthesised using inductive content analysis to identify recurring constructs, patterns and evidence gaps. The review is anticipated to commence in August 2026 and to be completed by September 2027. Ethics and dissemination Ethics approval is not required for this review of publicly available literature. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication, presentations to relevant Indigenous and public health partners, and knowledge products tailored to circumpolar surveillance planning.
authors: Ferwati, S., Seidler, I. K., Rodak, T., Crawford, A.

title: Exploring perspectives on implementing cervical length screening to prevent preterm birth in nulliparous women: protocol for the PRE-EMPT qualitative work packages
abstract: Introduction Preterm birth risk prediction currently relies on previous history, with those classified as intermediate-risk or high-risk being offered cervical length measurements. However, most preterm births occur in women considered low-risk. The majority of low-risk women are first-time mothers (nulliparous women) and therefore, typically do not receive cervical length measurements. Evidence from outside the UK suggests that cervical length screening and treatment with progesterone in low-risk women can prevent preterm birth. However, little is known about the acceptability and feasibility of introducing cervical length screening in low-risk nulliparous women in the UK National Health Service (NHS). This study aims to provide this evidence to inform decision-making for cervical length screening (NIHR PGfAR 207290). Methods and analysis A study consisting of two theoretically informed qualitative work packages will explore the perspectives and experiences of women, healthcare professionals and other relevant stakeholders regarding cervical length screening for low-risk nulliparous women. Data will be collected through a combination of semistructured interviews and focus groups with approximately 50 healthcare professionals and 50 women and an online survey. Women will be purposively sampled from community groups and maternity units. Healthcare professionals and providers will be identified through purposive and snowball sampling from maternity units and healthcare and other relevant organisations including those involved in the planning and commissioning of antenatal services. All interviews and focus groups will be audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Posters advertising the study will be displayed in maternity units and community centres. Data collection began in September 2025 and is due to end in December 2026. Data will first be analysed inductively and then deductively using the Behaviour Change Wheel, Theoretical Domains Framework and the Feasibility Framework. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval was granted by the Health Research Authority (IRAS 349196) and NHS Research Ethics Committee (25/NW/0252) as well as the University of Birmingham (RG_25-018). Findings will be shared with service users and healthcare providers through peer-reviewed publications and conferences. Results will also be reported to the UK National Screening Committee to inform recommendations on national adoption.
authors: Fox, C. E., Sykorova, M., Zafar, S., Carter, J., Kudrna, L., Jankovic, J., Grove, A., Leeson, C., Spence, T., Skrybant, M., Jones, E., Williams, E. V., Moorlock, S. J., MacArthur, C.

title: Professional and family caregivers perceptions of death literacy in end-of-life home care: a qualitative study
abstract: Background The growing prevalence of chronic diseases and population ageing have increased the need for end-of-life care, particularly in home settings. Death literacy, encompassing knowledge, skills, attitudes and emotional preparedness related to death and dying, is recognised as an important component of quality end-of-life care. However, little is known about caregivers’ perceptions of death literacy in the Iranian context. Objective To explore the perceptions of professional and family caregivers regarding death literacy in home-based end-of-life care. Methods This qualitative study used conventional content analysis based on Graneheim and Lundman’s approach. Data were collected through semistructured interviews with 12 professional and family caregivers involved in end-of-life care for patients with advanced chronic diseases in Tehran, Iran. Participants were recruited using purposive and snowball sampling. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed until data saturation was reached. Results Four core dimensions of death literacy emerged: (1) situational knowledge of dying, (2) experiential learning trajectory, (3) emotional reconciliation with death and (4) dignity-centred ethical practice. Two additional contextual domains (5) caregiver burden and relational challenges and (6) structural and organisational barriers described the relational and structural conditions in which death literacy was developed and enacted. Death literacy was described as a dynamic and culturally embedded process shaped by caregiving experiences, emotional engagement, informal learning, spirituality and interactions with families and the healthcare system. Conclusion Death literacy develops through lived experience, emotional reflection and cultural influences rather than formal education alone, while relational and structural conditions shape how these capacities are developed and enacted in practice. Educational, psychological and organisational support may strengthen caregiver preparedness and improve end-of-life care.
authors: Rezaei, M., Khaleghparast, S., Akhlaghi, E., Keshmiri, K., Asgari, M., Rostami, M., Shahrestanaki, S. K.

title: Assessing the believability of contraceptive misinformation among young Latinas (CREO): protocol for a discrete choice experiment
abstract: Introduction Contraceptive misinformation circulates widely on social media, and young Latinas are disproportionately exposed and more likely to internalise it, shaped by language barriers, limited institutional access and historical mistrust of the medical system. Prior work documents its prevalence and links influencer credibility to contraceptive behaviour, but which specific message features drive believability remains unknown. This protocol describes a discrete choice experiment (DCE), the first phase of the Choice and Reaction to Evaluate Online Opinions on Family Planning study, designed to identify which characteristics of contraceptive misinformation posts most influence perceived believability among young Latinas. Methods and analysis This is a cross-sectional online study using a visual DCE grounded in the Online Misinformation Engagement Framework. Six attributes across 19 levels (influencer type, contraceptive method, narrative type, side effect type, misinformation construct and tone) were retained from 13 candidates based on theoretical grounding, visual operationalisability and non-collinearity. A D-efficient fractional factorial design reduced 864 possible combinations to 32 profiles across 16 forced-choice pairs. Eligible participants (self-identified Latinas or Indigenous women from Latin America, aged 18–29, residing in the USA) will be recruited via targeted social media ads and will complete all 16 tasks, selecting the more believable of two simulated Instagram posts per pair. A target sample of 500 exceeds Johnson-Orme requirements for main and interaction effects. Conditional logit will serve as the primary analysis; mixed logit will be estimated as a secondary specification to assess preference heterogeneity. Ethics and dissemination This study was deemed exempt by the University of California, San Francisco Institutional Review Board (IRB #25-45383). Participants will provide informed consent and complete a structured debriefing correcting the misinformation presented in the DCE stimuli. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication, conference presentations and community forums serving Latinas, in English and Spanish.
authors: Abascal Miguel, L., Pfender, E., Gayer, S. G., Morse, S. M.

title: Clinician stakeholder priorities for improving the management of non-traumatic wrist disorders in the UK: a nominal group technique study
abstract: Introduction Increasingly detailed investigation confirms that the best management of those with non-traumatic wrist disorders (NTWD) remains elusive, and considerable potential for improvements to care exists. This study aimed to use a modified virtual nominal group technique (vNGT) to facilitate clinician stakeholder discussions to create consensus statements and recommend priorities for future improvements in the management of NTWD in the UK. Methods We created knowledge-gap topic areas and developed statements to reflect these. Preliminary ranking, silent reflection and idea generation occurred prior to the workshop. Two 2-hour vNGT workshops were conducted (n=8 and n=7; specialist hand therapists (8), first contact practitioners (2), generalist secondary care physiotherapists (2), wrist and hand specialist orthopaedic surgeons (2), specialist rheumatology physiotherapist) during which five nominal questions were discussed to create consensus statements (November 2025). Ranking of statements from all activities occurred 1 week following completion of the final workshop. Results Direction was given for key components of assessment noting that specific diagnosis should be attempted, and de Quervain’s tenosynovitis should be considered a distinct entity to grouped NTWD. Where specific diagnosis was deemed unattainable, a transition to a non-specific approach was recommended. Participants emphasised the importance of considering patient’s lived experience and functional goals when informing management decisions. Prognosis and self-management strategies should be prioritised, avoiding either over-investigation for non-specific problems or generic management for distinct treatable conditions. Conclusions UK-based clinician stakeholders, predominantly from secondary care, developed consensus-based priority statements regarding future improvements for the management of people with NTWD. Competing clinician perspectives were found regarding diagnostic specificity, resulting in apparently contradictory consensus priorities and highlighting underlying divisions in how NTWD are conceptualised and managed.
authors: Mitchell, T. G. C., Mallett, R., McLean, S., Hamilton, N., Dean, B., Peat, G.

title: Analysis of the impact of naturally-acquired immunity on Shigella vaccine performance to inform clinical trials: A simulation-based modeling study
abstract: by Avnika B. Amin, Maria Garcia Quesada, Daniel Trudell, Natalie E. Dean, Benjamin A. Lopman, James A. Platts-Mills, Elizabeth T. Rogawski McQuade Background Effective vaccines against Shigella , the leading bacterial cause of diarrheal disease globally, could prevent morbidity and mortality from shigellosis as well as limit antibiotic resistance. Several Shigella vaccine candidates are in late stages of development, and the design of large Phase 3 trials in target populations is underway. In high incidence settings, children are expected to rapidly accrue natural immunity such that after repeated pathogen exposure, unvaccinated infants may have similar levels of immunity as vaccinated infants. For this reason, in these settings estimates of vaccine efficacy (VE) may underestimate expected efficacy in a fully naïve population. To set expectations and support optimal planning of future Shigella vaccine trials, we aimed to quantify the potential impact of this phenomenon on VE estimates under different surveillance strategies and assumptions about Shigella immunity. Methods and findings We simulated Shigella vaccine trials in low-, medium-, and high-burden settings under different assumptions about vaccine- and infection-conferred immunity. We estimated VE against severe, Shigella -attributable disease and any Shigella -attributable diarrhea under six trial designs: active surveillance for Shigella infection or symptom-based reporting paired with single-outcome, stratified recurrent outcome, or crude recurrent-outcome Cox proportional hazards models. In each scenario, we evaluated bias, 95% confidence interval (CI) coverage, and the false negative rate. Only the trial design using active surveillance for infection and single outcome models was consistently unbiased across all examined scenarios. The other five designs underestimated VE by up to an absolute 20%, with a single outcome model paired with symptom-based reporting performing least poorly. Bias generally was worse at higher-burden sites. For realistically sized trials, the 95% CI coverage and false negative rate were also worse at higher-burden sites. The results were sensitive to input parameters which depended on assumptions about Shigella natural history based on limited published data. Conclusions The observed VE in Shigella vaccine trials is likely to underestimate true VE, though the magnitude of underestimation described here is conditional on the simulation’s inputs and assumptions. Careful trial design is needed to minimize this underestimation.
authors: Avnika B. Amin, Maria Garcia Quesada, Daniel Trudell, et al.

title: LEAF: benchmarking multiobjective evolutionary feature selection over large language model–extracted symptoms for interpretable Traditional Chinese Medicine respiratory syndrome differentiation
abstract: Differentiating Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) respiratory syndromes requires weighing overlapping symptoms together with tongue and pulse findings, a task that most AI systems for TCM perform end-to-end but without an interpretable intermediate representation. In this study, we addressed this gap with LEAF (LLM extraction and multiobjective feature selection), a two-stage modular framework evaluated on 3,253 records covering 14 respiratory syndromes from the TCM-SD benchmark. Its first large language model (LLM) stage extracted a 35-item symptom ontology that was built entirely from public TCM sources; among three interchangeable LLMs, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct was ranked as the best, followed by Phi-4 and the TCM domain model BianCang. Its second evolutionary-computation stage benchmarked four multiobjective evolutionary algorithms [non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II (NSGA-II), strength Pareto evolutionary algorithm 2 (SPEA2), competitive mechanism-based multiobjective particle swarm optimizer (CMOPSO), and non-dominated sorting differential evolution (NSDE)] over 10 seeds, and they were compared using Friedman’s and Nemenyi’s testing in terms of both classification outcome and search-process quality. The four algorithms showed no significant separation on held-out macro-F1, although NSDE led nominally, and none exceeded the full-feature baseline on point estimates. In contrast, hypervolume differed significantly and favored NSGA-II, the weakest of the four on held-out macro-F1. A four-classifier panel found no algorithm to be significantly different from either the full-feature baseline or a random-feature control, which was significantly outperformed only by the full-feature baseline. Applying NSDE to the remaining two LLM pipelines reproduced the original ranking, and its representative solution was fully attested against the knowledge base of TCM-SD, although not typically so across all the 10 seeds. These results show that an LLM-extraction frontend built exclusively from public knowledge can provide a representation over which evolutionary feature selection cuts the candidate feature set roughly in half without a statistically detectable cost in performance, albeit at a small point-estimate cost; that hypervolume and inverted generational distance are not reliable stand-ins for classification-relevant algorithm selection here; and that a no-gold-standard proxy evaluation can substitute human annotation when expert time is limited. Because both stages plug in and out freely, the framework can absorb stronger components in either stage as they become available.
authors: Xuanhang Luo, Huan Ding, Xize Zhang, et al.

title: Needs assessment to shape rural health research capacity building strategies: a mixed methods study
abstract: IntroductionRural areas require tailored rural health research capacity building aligned to the local needs and interests. To set the directions for a rural health research capacity building strategy, we aimed to conduct a needs assessment of rural health research interests, barriers and enablers across rural health stakeholders.MethodsWe conducted mixed methods research that included an anonymous online survey of Australian rural health stakeholders from hospitals, primary care and rural health agencies and qualitative interviews with those who consented from two rural regions in Victoria, Australia.ResultsForty individuals completed the survey and twenty-six individuals participated in interviews. The aggregate data suggested that there is strong interest in rural health research although many survey respondents preferred to be aware about research that is underway and which they could get involved in, rather than to lead it. Interview findings suggested that rural health research is considered useful for driving rural health investments, promoting quality healthcare and recruiting and retaining rural health workforces. Barriers to rural health research included higher workloads in smaller clinical teams, limited funding, under-developed research structures, organisation, time and tools. Enablers included having a research strategy aligned with the community's needs, research governance/planning processes for research teams, research tools and academic networks. The balance of interests, barriers and enablers for rural health research capacity building varied between rural health executives and clinicians but was consistent across hospitals and other rural health services.ConclusionsRural health research is valued for driving more investment, demonstrating rural healthcare service quality and recruiting and retaining health workforce. However, strategies to build research capacity may need to focus on helping rural health services formulate research strategies, structures, governance and funding and to embed tools and planning processes in collaboration with research teams at rural universities. Such capacity could facilitate engagement and participation of diverse rural stakeholders in flexible ways. Addressing rural health research needs also requires robust place-based academic and practice networks across rural regions.
authors: Belinda O’Sullivan, Anton Isaacs, Logan Westley, et al.

title: Relationship extraction for adverse drug events in clinical notes using large language models: a retrospective cross-sectional study
abstract: Publication date: November 2026 Source: eBioMedicine, Volume 133 Author(s): Joseph M. Plasek, Yiming Li, Mary G. Amato, Dinah Foer, Diane L. Seger, Shayma Alzaidi, Huiyuan Zhou, Gretchen Purcell Jackson, David W. Bates, Li Zhou
authors: Joseph M. Plasek, Yiming Li, Mary G. Amato, et al.

title: Critique of impure reason: Unveiling the reasoning behaviour of medical large language models
abstract: Despite the current ubiquity of large language models (LLMs) across the medical domain, there is a surprising lack of studies which address their reasoning behaviour . We emphasise the importance of understanding reasoning behaviour as opposed to high-level prediction accuracies, since it is equivalent to explainable AI (XAI) in this context. In particular, achieving XAI in medical LLMs used in the clinical domain will have a significant impact across the healthcare sector. Therefore, in this work, we adapt the existing concept of reasoning behaviour and articulate its interpretation within the specific context of medical LLMs. We survey and categorise current state-of-the-art approaches for modelling and evaluating reasoning in medical LLMs. Additionally, we propose theoretical frameworks which can empower medical professionals or machine learning engineers to gain insight into the low-level reasoning operations of these previously obscure models. We also outline key open challenges facing the development of large reasoning models . The subsequent increased transparency and trust in medical machine learning models by clinicians as well as patients will accelerate the integration, application as well as further development of medical AI for the healthcare system as a whole.
authors: Shamus Zi Yang Sim, Tyrone Chen

title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis
abstract: arXiv:2610.36325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.
authors: Roxana Ramona Szomiu, George Ursu, Adrian Groza

title: OA-RAG: Ontology-based Agentic RAG for Faithful LLM Reasoning
abstract: arXiv:2610.36335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well across many real-world tasks but remain prone to hallucination, limiting their reliability in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare, where answers must be grounded in established knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates this problem by incorporating external information, but often overlooks logical relationships and relies heavily on the LLM's own reasoning, which can compromise answer faithfulness. We propose OA-RAG, an agent that integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning, drawing on both the logical structure and informal annotations of domain ontologies. For each answer, OA-RAG reports the ontology observations used as evidence and a model-assessed grounding level (entailed, supported, related, or unrelated) that characterises the strength of that evidence. Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical question-answering tasks, OA-RAG achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods, with particularly strong results on reasoning-intensive tasks. The reported grounding levels also offer a useful indication of answer reliability, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy. Finally, our results demonstrate the value of ontologies as knowledge sources: OA-RAG is competitive with, and sometimes outperforms, domain-specific RAG systems that draw on sources such as textbooks.
authors: Hui Yang, Jiaoyan Chen, Yongsheng Gao

title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
abstract: arXiv:2610.36513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.
authors: Yibo Yang, Zerui Huang, Haomiao Yang, Zixia Wang

title: ReForest: Interpretability Meets Reasoning in Isolation Forest
abstract: arXiv:2610.37316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Statistical anomaly detection methods like Isolation Forest are efficient but suffer from a critical semantic gap. They identify numerical rarities but fail to understand the contextual meaning of data, often missing subtle, context-dependent anomalies. Conversely, Large Language Models possess strong semantic reasoning capabilities but are prohibitively expensive and slow for large-scale deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose ReForest, a novel framework that synergizes the statistical efficiency of Isolation Forest with the reasoning power of LLMs. ReForest transforms the latent decision paths of Isolation Forest into natural-language explanations, enabling an LLM to refine anomaly detection through an uncertainty-aware dynamic ensemble. This approach allows the model to adaptively weigh statistical and semantic signals based on uncertainty-driven instance-level confidence. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets (Healthcare, Finance) demonstrate that ReForest significantly outperforms baselines, achieving an average 21% improvement in Recall and a 10% gain in F1-score. Our framework not only improves detection performance but also enhances model transparency by grounding semantic narratives in statistical evidence, providing interpretable rationales essential for high-stakes decision-making.
authors: Juyoung Seo, Geonwoo Bang, Dongho Kim, Moohong Min

title: MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine
abstract: arXiv:2610.36006v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: System One decision models such as Jev answer structured questions in a single forward pass without generating text, offering fast and computationally efficient clinical decision support. We evaluate MedJev, an open System One model that runs locally on a laptop, across ten medical benchmarks spanning medical knowledge, diagnosis, and patient level prediction using MIMIC IV and MIMIC IV ED. We compare MedJev against zero shot LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models. MedJev achieves accuracies of 72.5 percent on MedQA, 75.4 percent on USMLE, and 80.1 percent on NEJM, approaching published GPT 4 performance while maintaining well calibrated confidence estimates (ECE 0.028 to 0.063). On patient level tasks, MedJev achieves an AUROC of 0.926 for In Hospital Mortality, exceeding XGBoost (0.902), but underperforms supervised models on operational outcomes such as ED Triage Admission (0.745 vs. 0.809). Patient level predictions also exhibit substantial miscalibration (In Hospital Mortality ECE 0.286). We introduce a lightweight, two parameter recalibration method that adapts predictions to local patient populations using 50 to 200 labeled examples, reducing ECE to 0.007. Our findings establish open System One models as a promising zero shot baseline for medical AI, combining competitive predictive performance with low computational cost and efficient local calibration. We release our code and evaluation harness to support future research.
authors: Simon A. Lee, Jiahang Sha, Moonseong Jeong, Yunbei Pan, Jeffrey N. Chiang

title: Dense Representation Learning and Differentiable Shape Modeling for Spine Landmark Detection
abstract: arXiv:2610.36951v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spine landmark detection from spinal X-ray is a key step for estimating spine deformation severity, for building biomechanical models, and for pre-operative planning. We reframe anatomical landmark detection as a pixel-level contrastive representation learning problem, matching dense pixel embeddings with landmark prototypes. Surprisingly, even with a generic U-Net backbone, this formulation results in more discriminative heatmaps compared to the traditional heatmap regression paradigm, leading to improved discrimination between vertebral corners on distinct vertebra. Furthermore, we combine the resulting heatmaps with learnable shape priors over the global configuration of spinal landmarks to resolve ambiguities in landmark locations, yielding a simple and practical approach to spinal landmark detection. Our approach is competitive, in terms of landmark accuracy and clinical parameter estimation, with the state-of-the-art on the public AASCE dataset and on two private spinal X-ray datasets. Our code and pre-trained weights are available at https://github.com/BioMedTP/Pix2Point.
authors: Augustin Daridon, Sofiane Sifaoui, Ayman Assi, Mohamad Karam, Wafa Skalli, Elsa Angelini, Loic Le Folgoc

title: When Rubrics Fail: Hallucinations Reveal Blind Spots in Medical AI Evaluation
abstract: arXiv:2609.12718v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hallucinations can undermine clinician trust in LLMs, making it important that evaluation methods capture clinically relevant errors. Rubric-based evaluation has become the leading approach for assessing LLMs in medicine, but it is unclear whether rubric scores reflect such errors. We first study this in a controlled setting using MedHallu, finding that more specific rubrics better distinguish correct from hallucinated responses. To test this systematically, we develop a taxonomy of medical hallucination types and a clinician-validated error-injection pipeline that creates matched correct and error-injected responses. Across HealthBench, HealthBench Professional, and LiveMedBench, our clinically relevant hallucinations are missed by rubrics, often leaving scores unchanged. We find that rubrics are most effective when explicitly checking facts, and are less effective for additional or unexpected errors they do not anticipate. A preliminary retrieval-based factuality check recovers some of the rubric-blind errors, suggesting a complementary approach. These findings reveal systematic blind spots in current medical evaluation of LLMs and suggest that rubric scores alone are insufficient to establish clinical reliability, potentially undermining clinician trust and confidence in clinical deployment.
authors: Griffin Farrow, Lily Sijia Li, Jack Johnson, Tingyan Wang, Philip Torr, William Bolton, Fabio J. Fehr

title: Synthetic Hospital: An Open, Verifiable, Physician-Validated Longitudinal EHR Benchmark
abstract: arXiv:2609.30027v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frontier language models are rarely used in clinical workflows because the realistic, longitudinal benchmarks needed to develop them are scarce. Real electronic health record (EHR) data cannot be openly shared due to privacy, ethics or data use issues and it does not contain verifiable ground truth since the chart records only reflect what clinicians documented. We introduce Synthetic Hospital, an open, fully synthetic, fact-grounded longitudinal EHR benchmark that resolves the open sharing and verifiable ground truth barriers. Built entirely from public medical-education material with no protected health information, it comprises 1,268 longitudinal patients and 5,602 encounters, where every diagnosis, finding, and temporal relation is grounded in standard ontologies (ICD-10-CM, SNOMED CT, LOINC) and with a complete provenance chain back to its source medical education material. Synthetic Hospital is served through a simulated hospital record system that mirrors real EHR infrastructure (standard interoperability APIs, role-based access and function-calling interface). In a blinded review, physicians distinguished its records from real patient charts at near-chance rates (53%). Across 10 frontier and open models, none approaches ceiling: the best model reconstructs a patient's longitudinal problem list with a severity-weighted F1 of 0.73, level with the mean of seven physicians on a matched subset but well below the best of them (0.89), and misses roughly half of clinically relevant findings when summarizing a chart. Overall, these results highlight that Synthetic Hospital is a difficult and realistic test of clinical AI performance.
authors: Christine Park, Valerie Chen, Tim Dettmers

title: Counting Clues: A Lightweight Probabilistic Baseline Can Match an LLM
abstract: arXiv:2512.12868v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on multiple-choice clinical diagnosis benchmarks, yet it is unclear how much of this performance reflects underlying probabilistic reasoning. We study this through questions from MedQA that ask for the most likely diagnosis. We introduce Frequency-Based Probabilistic Ranker (FBPR), a lightweight method that scores options with a smoothed Naive Bayes over concept-diagnosis co-occurrence statistics from a large corpus. When co-occurrence statistics are sourced from Dolma, the pretraining corpus for OLMo, and RedPajama, an open reproduction of the LLaMA pretraining-data recipe, FBPR achieves comparable performance to the corresponding LLMs. Furthermore, direct LLM inference and FBPR exhibit complementary strengths, correctly answering largely different subsets of questions with overlap barely above chance. Combining them with a simple hybrid method yields a notable gain over either method alone. These findings show that explicit probabilistic baselines can account for a substantial portion of the benchmark performance on diagnosis questions, while serving as historically grounded reference points and complementary signals for hybridization.
authors: Furong Jia, Yuan Pu, Finn Guo, Monica Agrawal

title: Clinical Note Bloat Reduction for Efficient LLM Use
abstract: arXiv:2604.16364v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Background: Clinical notes contain extensive duplicated text from templates, copy-paste, and auto-populated fields ("note bloat"), diluting clinical signal, limiting longitudinal context, and increasing large language model (LLM) costs. Methods: TRACE removes note bloat using note-level EHR metadata to identify templated and copied content, with frequency-based de-duplication when metadata are unavailable. We evaluated TRACE using blinded physician span review and gold-standard templated-text annotations across four cohorts spanning liver transplant, obstetrics, and inpatient populations at multiple health systems (5.3M notes). We compared zero-shot LLMs and embedding-based classifiers using original and TRACE-processed notes for 20 information extraction tasks and prediction of 5-year survival, postpartum hemorrhage, and 30-day readmission. Results: Only 0.3-6.6% of removed text was flagged as author-generated; TRACE captured 86% of annotated templated characters. Information extraction F1 differences averaged by cohort ranged from -0.009 to +0.004; task-specific prediction F1 differences ranged from -0.011 to +0.018. Among 1,000 randomly sampled Stanford Health Care patients, TRACE reduced chart text by 47.3% (742.7M characters), averaging 220,167 fewer tokens per patient. Using 2024 encounter volumes at a large tertiary academic center and one query per encounter, projected three-year net savings ranged from $1.00M to $13.58M across evaluated model pricing schemes, including initial and annual TRACE processing costs. Conclusion: TRACE substantially reduces clinical note redundancy while preserving information extraction and prediction performance. Underused EHR metadata can reduce LLM inference costs, expand usable longitudinal context, and support scalable clinical AI.
authors: Jordan L. Cahoon, Chloe Stanwyck, Asad Aali, Rachel Madding, Sulaiman S. Somani, Emma Sun, Yixing Jiang, Renumathy Dhanasekaran, Emily Alsentzer

title: PRISM: Pathology Reliability In Scarce-label Medicine. A Tile-level Benchmark of Pathology Foundation Models
abstract: arXiv:2610.36517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pathology foundation models are typically benchmarked on classification performance at full label availability and on in-distribution test sets, while calibration, behavior at low label budgets, and robustness under cross-institutional shift are seldom evaluated jointly. We introduce PRISM, a tile-level benchmark that measures the reliability of pathology foundation models along four axes: model choice, label fraction, calibration, and out-of-distribution transfer. PRISM evaluates eight foundation models (CLIP, PLIP, CONCH, UNI, Virchow2, GigaPath, H-Optimus-0, Midnight) on six tile-level datasets at six label fractions (1% to 100%) with three seeds (864 linear probe runs), extended with a five-hospital Camelyon17 study of 20 directed transfer pairs. Four phenomena emerge. (i) Under full supervision, AUROC rank predicts post-temperature calibration rank consistently across datasets (Spearman rho = 0.52, I^2 = 0%), whereas at 1% labels the relationship becomes dataset-specific (rho = -0.24, I^2 = 67%). (ii) On harder datasets the linear probe collapses to a single predicted class below a dataset-specific label fraction. (iii) Whether additional source-domain labels help or harm target calibration tracks how well the probe transfers: below a transfer AUROC of roughly 0.85, more labels worsen target ECE in 86-88% of combinations. (iv) Temperature scaling fails to reduce ECE in 49 of 288 cells, miscalibration is predominantly under-confidence, and a source-fitted temperature is harmful under failing transfer. PRISM is released as a pip-installable package with reference results for all 288 cells. Code and data: https://github.com/alicemkyn/prism-benchmark

title: Systematic Morphometric Brain Autoencoding for Representation Learning in Neurodegenerative Diseases
abstract: arXiv:2610.37074v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Early identification of neurodegenerative disorders using structural T1-weighted MRI is essential for timely clinical intervention, yet supervised deep learning models often struggle to generalize due to limited annotations and scanner-induced distribution shift. Self-supervised learning offers a promising alternative; however, existing approaches are largely adapted from natural image paradigms, relying on contrastive objectives or generic masked reconstruction with voxel-wise losses, which may not fully capture the distributed morphometric patterns associated with neurodegeneration. We introduce SYMBA (SYstematic Morphometric Brain Autoencoding), a self-supervised pretraining framework specifically designed for structural brain MRI. SYMBA integrates anatomically constrained masking, a multi-scale structural similarity (MS-SSIM) reconstruction objective, and a progressive curriculum that transitions from local anatomical detail to global brain morphology. These components explicitly incorporate neuroanatomical structure into the self-supervised objective rather than relying on generic image priors. Pretrained on 6,953 T1-weighted MRI scans from nine heterogeneous cohorts, SYMBA is evaluated using frozen linear probing on two independent unseen datasets, enabling a strict assessment of out-of-distribution generalization. Across multiple clinical tasks, SYMBA consistently outperforms recent neuroimaging foundation models, achieving 0.930 AUROC for Alzheimer's disease classification, 0.772 for mild cognitive impairment conversion prediction, and strong performance in amyloid status prediction. In low-label regimes, SYMBA demonstrates high sample efficiency, reaching approximately 0.90 AUROC for AD/CN classification using only six labeled subjects.

title: The impact of heatwaves on maternal, neonatal and child health outcomes in Western Australian climate zones: A protocol paper for a retrospective cohort study [version 3; peer review: 2 approved, 1 approved with reservations, 1 not approved]
abstract: Background Rising global temperatures have resulted in an increase in the frequency and severity of heatwaves. Pregnancy is a time of substantial physiological change and thus maternal and neonatal health outcomes are susceptible to adverse effects of heat. There is a lack of knowledge about thermoregulation in pregnancy, including how effectively pregnant people adapt in different climate contexts and what specific environmental conditions present the largest thermoregulatory challenges. The primary aim of this study is to examine the associations between exposure to heatwaves during pregnancy and maternal, neonatal, and child health outcomes in Western Australia climatic regions. Methods All neonates born in Western Australia between 1991 and 2023 will be identified from perinatal records (~960,000 neonates). Perinatal records will be linked to weather data from the ERA5 database using Statistical Area 2 geocoding to identify heatwave exposed pregnancies. Commonly used definitions of heatwave exposure will be tested against three neonatal outcomes (pre-term birth, low birth weight, and congenital anomalies). From this, a single or small number of definition will be selected to examine maternal, neonatal, and child health outcomes using linked hospital, emergency department, and education assessment data, as well as data from the Western Australian congenital anomalies and death register. The association between heatwaves during pregnancy and health outcomes will be performed using generalised estimating equations, adjusting for covariates including, but not limited to, cigarette smoking, parity, maternal age, socio-economic status, and Aboriginality where appropriate. Stratification by socio-economic status and geographic region will also be carried out. Discussion Examining the association between exposure to heatwaves in pregnancy and maternal, neonatal and child outcomes is important given the increasing frequency of heatwaves. The study will highlight which heat definitions confers the highest vulnerability as well as demographic and geographic subgroups who are particularly vulnerable to the effects of heatwaves. It will provide valuable information for future public health planning, including targets for intervention.

title: Challenges and lessons learned in a multicenter emerging neuroinfections study in Colombia: A pathfinder study [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
abstract: Background Multicenter research studies in low-and middle-income countries face complex operational, methodological, and logistical challenges that are rarely documented systematically. The Emerging Neuroinfections in the Americas Study (NEAS) is a 10-year multicenter research project in Colombia. The Pathfinder methodology was applied to map research processes, identify challenges, and generate transferable lessons from NEAS. Methods A multi-method design combining in parallel a systematic document analysis and key informant interviews was used. A process map was constructed to organize findings across the planning and execution phases of NEAS, covering data collection, biological sample management, and clinical follow-up. Qualitative evidence was analyzed thematically around three operational axes: clinical data management, handling and storage of biological samples, and participants follow-up. Results NEAS originated as a public health emergency response to the 2015–2016 Zika epidemic, subsequently transitioning into a fully structured study. The protocol underwent continuous adaptation, including incorporation of COVID19 pandemic procedures. Annual turnover of study physicians required structured boarding protocols. There were gaps in a formal data management plan. Sample loss risks were minimized by implementing standardized procedures (SOPs), physician verification and project manager-led quality control. International alliances were critical for sustainability. A stakeholder map was developed identifying stakeholders across a power–interest matrix. Conclusions Long-term multicenter research in Colombia is feasible but requires robust governance structures, flexible yet standardized protocols, sustained international partnerships, and systematic documentation practices. The lessons generated are transferable to other studies in Latin America and the Caribbean, contributing to the growing capacity to conduct research in response to global health emergencies.

title: Process evaluation protocol of a trial evaluating app-based post knee arthroplasty telerehabilitation strategy in India [version 3; peer review: 2 approved]
abstract: Background Physical rehabilitation after knee arthroplasty is essential for improving functional outcomes. However, adherence to rehabilitation is poor. We developed a multicomponent mobile application TeleREhabilitation after knee ArThroplasty (TReAT app) comprising education, exercise videos, an e-diary for self-monitoring progress, two-way communication, and remote therapy planning to facilitate home-based rehabilitation. The TReAT trial is a 1:1 randomized controlled superiority trial to evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of the intervention against usual care, with an embedded process evaluation. This paper reports the protocol for process evaluation. Methods and analysis Consenting individuals undergoing knee arthroplasty at a public and private tertiary care hospital in Delhi, who are able to use a smartphone will be randomized to either app-based or usual home-based rehabilitation and followed up at 3 and 6 months to assess knee-related functional outcomes. A mixed-methods convergent parallel design supported by a logic model will be used for a process evaluation. Data from screening log, backend app analytics, interviews with end users, and researcher notes will contribute to the evaluation based on RE-AIM framework. Researcher notes will be quantified and, consolidated with app analytics to summarise fidelity, and adoption. Thematic analysis of interviews will provide insights into contextual factors influencing intervention adoption during the trial and intention to use the TReAT app beyond the trial period. To explore potential association between use of intervention components and outcomes, correlations between functional outcomes, knowledge score and rehabilitation self-efficacy will be examined. Conclusions The process evaluation will provide insights into the potential uptake and scalability of TReAT intervention. Comparing findings across public and private healthcare settings will enhance understanding of how the intervention functions in different contexts. The findings will inform implementation strategies to improve rehabilitation care using mHealth interventions in India. Trial registration The trial was registered prospectively with the Clinical Trial Registry of India (CTRI/2024/06/068838).

title: When are large language models medical devices? Navigating the MDR and AI Act for healthcare applications
abstract: The flexibility of generative artificial intelligence (AI), and specifically large language models (LLMs), holds promise to transform healthcare by offering new tools to improve patient care and enhance clinician efficiency. However, this flexibility introduces new challenges, as LLM applications might inadvertently be used in ways that do not align with the intended purpose of the manufacturer, raising patient safety concerns and liability issues. We have identified a regulatory gap whereby LLM applications that could be repurposed, malfunction or be inadvertently misused for medical purposes fall outside the scope of the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) because they lack a medical intended purpose, and outside meaningful AI Act safety obligations because they do not qualify as high-risk systems, yet still present patient safety risks without adequate regulatory guidance. In this manuscript, we aim to address this regulatory gap for LLM applications in healthcare by identifying these ambiguous grey-area applications and providing four recommendations—validation, mitigation, compliance and alignment—focused on prevention and risk mitigation rather than reclassification as medical devices. These recommendations are intended to advance the responsible implementation of LLM applications in healthcare while ensuring patient safety.
