title: What can chatbot conversations reveal about vaccine concerns? An observational topic modelling study for public health infoveillance
abstract: Objective The COVID-19 pandemic was marked by a surge of online information, including misinformation about vaccines. Health agencies recommend infoveillance to track public attitudes on immunisation, particularly during health emergencies. We sought to investigate how chatbots may serve as a novel data source for digital monitoring of vaccine concerns. Chatbots are an increasingly popular two-way health communication tool, and an analysis of anonymised chatbot inputs could identify emerging misinformation and public concerns. Methods and analysis We used a topic modeller and large language model (LLM)-based few-shot learner to understand the themes and emotional tone of chats users sent to the Vaccine Information Resource Assistant (VIRA), a non-generative chatbot created by Johns Hopkins to answer questions about COVID-19 vaccines that was used or shared by health departments in 12 US states. We employed BERTopic to conduct topic modelling on user textual data and conversations. We also used OpenAI’s LLM, GPT-4o, employing a human-labelled set of chats and instructions to help fine-tune the model and to classify a random subset of 8760 chats sent to VIRA into pro-vaccine, neutral and anti-vaccine. Results Analysing 30 336 chats users sent to VIRA over a 2-year period, in English and Spanish, we found most focused on vaccine recommendations and safety (71%), with far fewer chats addressing conspiracies and questioning the need for vaccines (3%). Sentiment analysis of a randomly selected subset of chats (n=8760) indicated that English-language chats were more likely than Spanish-language chats to express negative emotions about vaccines (12% vs 4%), but the majority of messages sent by users in either language were classified as neutral. Conclusion This observational analysis offers a detailed case study on how anonymised chatbot dialogues may expand on insights from social media for health agencies and others seeking to monitor opinions and work to support strong vaccine confidence. As chatbots become increasingly fluid conversational tools, the findings suggest significant potential for chatbot-facilitated health interventions, both for public engagement as well as understanding.
authors: Novello, P., Weeks, R., Sedoc, J., Ou, Y., Sangha, P., Miller, E., Jamison, A., Agarwal, S.

title: COPE: Chain-of-Thought Prediction Engine for open-source large language model-based stroke outcome prediction from clinical notes
abstract: Objective To develop and evaluate Chain-of-Thought Outcome Prediction Engine (COPE), a reasoning-enhanced large language model, for predicting 90-day functional outcomes after acute ischaemic stroke (AIS) from unstructured clinical notes. Methods We included 464 patients with AIS who had discharge summaries and 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) outcomes. COPE uses a two-step chain-of-thought (CoT) framework based on sequential open-source models (LLaMA-3-8B): the first generates intermediate clinical reasoning and the second outputs an mRS prediction. We compared COPE’s performance with GPT-4.1, ClinicalBERT, a structured variable-based machine learning model (XGBoost) and a single-step large language model (LLM) without CoT. Performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE), accuracy within ±1 mRS point (±1 ACC) and exact accuracy (ACC). Results COPE achieved an MAE of 1.01 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.11), ±1 ACC of 74.4% (95% CI 69.9% to 78.8%) and ACC of 32.8% (95% CI 28.0% to 37.6%), comparable to GPT-4.1 (MAE, 1.00 (95% CI 0.90 to 1.09); ±1 ACC, 77.9% (95% CI 73.7% to 82.0%); ACC, 32.5% (95% CI 28.0% to 37.4%); p=0.72, 0.11 and 0.96). COPE demonstrated performance comparable to a strong structured-data baseline using XGBoost (MAE, 1.03 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.13); ±1 ACC, 73.9% (95% CI 69.4% to 78.5%); ACC, 33.3% (95% CI 28.5% to 38.2%); p=0.77, 0.87 and 0.89), and outperformed ClinicalBERT and the single-step LLM. Subgroup analyses showed consistent performance across sex and age, with higher error among older patients, those undergoing thrombectomy and those with longer summaries. Conclusions COPE, a reasoning-enhanced framework using lightweight, open-source LLMs, achieved performance comparable to a proprietary model and to strong traditional baselines while operating without model retraining or manual feature engineering. It offers an accurate and privacy-preserving solution for outcome prediction from unstructured clinical text.
authors: Liu, Y., Feng, H., Jiang, B., Wang, Y., Wintermark, M., Liebeskind, D., Moseley, M., Lansberg, M., Albers, G., Heit, J., Zaharchuk, G.

title: From bedside to bench: towards clinical predictive AI research that achieves real-world impact
abstract: Clinical predictive artificial intelligence (AI) tools, including equations or models developed using statistical, machine learning or AI methods, have proliferated, yet relatively few effectively translate into routine care. A major contributor to this bench-to-bedside gap is the lack of explicit translational planning at the outset. In this narrative review, we synthesise emerging principles for designing, developing and evaluating predictive AI tools with real-world impact in mind. We propose a pre-modelling discipline that defines the clinical question, intended users and position in the care pathway, highlights the importance of early and sustained stakeholder engagement and explicitly links programme theory to model outputs to inform decisions and change outcomes. It covers regulatory pathways and routes to self-sustainability, ethical and equity considerations and software implementation requirements that shape whether tools can be deployed and sustained. Finally, we summarise core methodological issues in model development, validation and monitoring that are particularly relevant to translation. Taken together, this bedside-to-bench approach reconceptualises clinical predictive AI tools as complex interventions, beginning with a clear expectation of their real-world deployment and benefit and planning backwards to inform model development. This shift in thinking is required to increase the chance that clinical predictive AI tools deliver real-world benefit rather than remaining confined to print.
authors: Si, S., Collins, G. S., Alderman, J. E., Van Calster, B., Wynants, L., Broome, M. R., Daw, P., Denniston, A. K., Ensor, J., Perry, B. I.

title: Understanding digital inclusion through the transformation of services and users: a narrative review and novel framework
abstract: The move towards digitally enabled healthcare offers the opportunity to deliver better care for all. Despite this potential, existing evidence suggests the same widely reported health inequalities that currently impact underserved populations are retained and often exacerbated by digital health services. In an attempt to overcome this digital divide, the related concept of digital inclusion has emerged that describes the policies, commissioning, and service-level actions and interventions necessary to address the issue. However, existing frameworks which have attempted to describe and understand digital inclusion have failed to reflect the evolution of organisations, services and users over time. Understanding inclusivity through the lens of digital transformation offers one way of providing a more accurate reflection of how contextual influences on digital inclusion relating to users, organisational processes and broader policy level interventions evolve temporally. The work presented here describes a novel framework for digital inclusion that combines the recognised elements of the digital divide with the core principles of digital transformation. The framework provides a multilevel understanding of how policy, organisations, communities and individuals combine and interact over time and successfully provides a unified means of developing and delivering more holistic strategies better equipped to address sustained digital inclusion. The framework is supported by a structured narrative review that provides exemplar evidence that underpins its constructs and theoretical position.
authors: Litchfield, I., Shukla, D., Greenfield, S.

title: The Long road to AI-physician partnership starts with learners: a map for AI in medical education
abstract: Medical students and residents are already using generative artificial intelligence (AI) to draft notes, summarise records and generate differential diagnoses, often informally and without institutional oversight. Adoption has outpaced policy and pedagogical processes, which makes restriction an unrealistic response. The practical question is how to integrate these tools so that clinical skills are not replaced as they are being built. We aim to give medical educators a practical guide for judging which uses of generative AI support skill formation at each stage of training and which displace it. Three distinct harms are at stake: deskilling, the erosion of acquired competencies; never-skilling, the failure to develop foundational skills when AI performs them before learners do; and mis-skilling, the absorption of AI-generated errors and biases as accurate practice. To calibrate integration, we propose a framework built on cognitive displacement, the degree to which a tool takes over the reasoning that training is designed to build. Appropriate use depends on a task’s position on that spectrum and the learner’s stage. Applied across the training continuum, the framework locates each risk where it has the greatest potential for harm. Never-skilling threatens preclinical students who have not yet built the competencies that AI could erode. Deskilling threatens residents, whose judgement is still consolidating. Mis-skilling arises wherever biased tools meet trainees making unsupervised decisions. Because the framework’s stage-specific predictions remain largely untested, we set out an agenda for measuring these risks prospectively. The principle is calibration, not prohibition. The open question is who designs that integration, and when.
authors: Patel, N., Kumar, A., Chi, J., Keet, K., Kugler, J., Hom, J., Hosamani, P.

title: Developing the i-MoMCARE application in Cambodia: an iterative co-design approach using rapid prototyping
abstract: Objective To develop a mobile health (mHealth) application (i-MoMCARE app) to support village health support groups (VHSGs) and health centre staff in delivering maternal and child health (MCH) services in rural Cambodia. Methods and analysis We adopted a co-design strategy to guide the development of the i-MoMCARE app. In phase 1, key stakeholders identified and proposed app features based on research-informed end-user needs. Phase 2 involved prioritising high-impact features for app development. In phase 3, VHSGs and health centre staff participated in usability testing of the i-MoMCARE app. Interview data collected through rapid qualitative interviews were thematically analysed. Results Sixteen stakeholders participated in phases 1 and 2 and 10 users participated in phase 3. The i-MoMCARE app comprises five core features: (1) clinical decision support system (CDSS), (2) electronic medical record (EMR) system, (3) educational resources, (4) digital worklog sorting and (5) offline functionality. Users reported that the CDSS improved consistency of care and boosted clinical confidence while the EMR enhanced data accuracy and retrieval efficiency. Educational resources were valued for supporting self-learning and community education. Meanwhile, worklog sorting improved time management and manpower planning, whereas offline functionality helped to ensure continued usage by mitigating connectivity issues. In addition, participants recognised the app’s potential to extend beyond clinical functions, highlighting its role in streamlining administrative tasks such as inventory tracking and automated reporting. Conclusions This study demonstrates the value of CDSS and EMR systems in supporting VHSGs and health centre staff in their daily operations. Supplementing these with educational and administrative features further increases the app’s utility, positioning it as a comprehensive tool for advancing the delivery of MCH services in resource-limited settings.
authors: Goh, H., Dary, C., Ung, M., Khuon, D., Oy, S., Chhay, S. C. A., Khim, C., Lee, Y. F., Kim, R., Saphonn, V., Yi, S.

title: Benchmarking large language models and clinicians using locally generated primary healthcare vignettes in Kenya
abstract: Objective To determine the ability of large language models (LLMs) to answer open-ended healthcare questions (rather than multiple-choice questions) accurately in a low-resource setting. Methods and analysis We benchmarked five LLMs (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash, DeepSeek-R1, MedGemma and o3) against Kenyan clinicians, using a randomly subsampled dataset of 507 vignettes (from a larger pool of 5107 clinical scenarios) spanning 12 nursing competency categories. Blinded physician panels rated responses using a 5-point Likert scale on an 11-domain rubric covering accuracy, safety, contextual appropriateness, and communication. We summarised mean scores and used Bayesian ordinal logistic regression to estimate probabilities of high-quality ratings (≥4) and to perform pairwise comparisons between LLMs and clinicians. Results Clinician mean ratings were lower than those for LLMs in 9/11 domains: 2.86 vs 4.25–4.72 (guideline alignment), 2.76 vs 4.25–4.73 (expert knowledge), 2.96 vs 4.30–4.73 (logical coherence) and 2.58 vs 4.16–4.68 (low omission of critical information). On safety-related domains, LLMs received higher ratings: minimal extent of possible harm 3.16 vs 4.29–4.68; low likelihood of harm 3.68 vs 4.54–4.81. Performance was similar for low inclusion of irrelevant content (4.28 vs 4.25–4.35) and for avoidance of demographic bias (4.86 vs 4.91–4.94). In Bayesian models, LLMs had >90% probability of ratings ≥4 in most domains, whereas clinicians exceeded 90% only for contextual relevance and demographic/socioeconomic bias. Pairwise contrasts showed broadly overlapping credible intervals among LLMs, with o3 leading numerically most domains except contextual relevance, demographic/socio-economic bias and relevance to the question. Generating all LLM responses cost US$3.86–US$8.68 per model (US$0.008–US$0.017 per vignette), compared with US$3.35 per clinician-generated vignette. Conclusions In controlled vignette-based tasks, LLMs produced responses that were more accurate, safer and more structured than clinicians, suggesting LLMs may have potential as supplementary knowledge and safety support tools. Findings support further evaluation in real patient encounters to determine effectiveness, safety and integration into clinical workflows, particularly in resource-constrained health systems.

title: Exposing the fragility of LLM reasoning through bias-inducing prompts: evidence from BiasMedQA
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the impact of large language model (LLM) reasoning on model susceptibility to cognitive bias-inducing prompts. Methods and analysis The performance of Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-32B and Gemini-2.5-Flash, along with their reasoning-enhanced variants, was evaluated in the public BiasMedQA dataset developed to evaluate seven established cognitive biases in 1273 clinical case vignettes. Each model was tested using a base prompt, a debiasing prompt with the instruction to actively mitigate cognitive bias and a few-shot prompt with additional sample cases of biased responses. Beyond the seven biases from BiasMedQA, Gemini-2.5-Flash was additionally tested using four unpublished bias-inducing prompts to unveil signs of potential data contamination and actively investigate brittleness. For each model pair, two mixed-effects logistic regression models were fitted to determine the impact of biases and mitigation strategies on performance. Results In all three models, the reasoning-enhanced variant achieved higher rates of correct responses (Llama-3.3-70B: 72.5–82.1% vs 61.0–73.4%, Qwen3-32B: 71.7–78.7% vs 55.5–64.1%, Gemini-2.5-Flash: 81.8–88.6% vs 80.0–83.7%). The performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash dropped considerably when exposing it to four additional unpublished bias-inducing prompts (from 80.0–88.6% to 47.4–86.1%), hinting at potential contamination of its training data and exposing underlying brittleness. In Llama-3.3-70B and Gemini-2.5-Flash, reasoning amplified model vulnerability to several bias-inducing prompts, while reasoning reduced susceptibility of Qwen3-32B to one of the seven biases. The debiasing and few-shot prompting approaches demonstrated statistically significant reductions in biased responses across all three model architectures. Conclusion In none of the three LLMs, reasoning was able to consistently reduce vulnerability to bias-inducing prompts, revealing the fragility of the reasoning capabilities purported by the model developers.
authors: Kim, S. H., Ziegelmayer, S., Busch, F., Mertens, C. J., Keicher, M., Adams, L. C., Bressem, K. K., Braren, R., Makowski, M. R., Kirschke, J. S., Hedderich, D. M., Wiestler, B.

title: Mixed-methods evaluation of clinician experiences and adoption patterns of an EHR-integrated generative AI-based clinical decision support uptake by clinicians in Kenya
abstract: Objective To quantify the patterns of uptake of a large language model (LLM)-based clinical decision support system across private primary health facilities in Kenya (operated by Penda Health) and explore factors influencing clinician uptake and overall experience. Methods and analysis A mixed-methods study combining quantitative analysis of clinical decision support system (CDSS) metadata from all consultations that took place between 1 February and 1 October 2024, augmented by qualitative data from 42 staff members (26 clinical officers, 10 facility managers, 4 nurses, 1 quality assurance manager and 1 business analyst). Data collection included journey mapping interviews (n=7), user-experience interviews (n=25), focus groups (n=2) and system utilisation metrics. Quantitative data were summarised using descriptive statistics, and qualitative data were analysed using thematic analysis (drawing on established theories of technology adoption and change management). Results In total, there were 258 106 clinical episodes across all Penda Health facilities over the 8-month observation period, of which 56 050 (21.7%) were augmented by use of the ‘artificial intelligence (AI) Consult’. ‘AI Consult’ use aggregated across the 16 facilities increased from 4% to 47% over 8 months. Clinicians provided feedback on their experience using the AI Consult in 31% of the clinical episodes; nearly all the feedback provided (99.5%) was positive. The qualitative investigation identified five key themes associated with clinicians’ experiences with the AI Consult tool: (1) there are several value propositions to an ‘AI Consult’ style tool, (2) clinicians’ confidence in the AI Consult grew with time, (3) clinicians’ application of the ‘AI Consult’ is influenced by case complexity, (4) responses from the AI Consult are largely believed and valued by clinicians but several improvements are recommended and (5) clinicians find the ‘AI Consult’ easy to use but identified several pain points that warrant attention. Conclusion Successful generative AI/LLM-enhanced CDSS implementation in resource-constrained settings requires: (1) robust technological infrastructure, (2) localisation to reflect clinical guidelines, (3) structured change management with clinical champions and (4) seamless workflow integration. Future product development exercises should specifically consider alternatives to active solicitation of CDSS input, as it is liable to overconfidence-related underutilisation.
authors: Obongo, C., Njenga, G., Otiangala, D., Jepleting, E., Wairimu, S., Emmanuel-Fabula, M., Kiptinness, S., Korom, R., Taliesin, B., Mateen, B. A.

title: Public perceptions of health data sharing for artificial intelligence research: a qualitative focus group study in the UK
abstract: Objective Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare offers potential to improve diagnosis, patient care and system efficiency. However, AI development, evaluation and post-implementation monitoring require large volumes of health data, and public trust is essential for enabling such data sharing. This study aimed to explore UK public perceptions of health data sharing for AI research, and to identify factors influencing willingness to participate. Methods and analysis We conducted eight 90-min online focus groups in May–July 2024, with 41 purposively sampled adult (18 years or older) members of the UK public, recruited via a national registry and departmental social media. Groups were selected to maximise diversity in age, ethnicity, household income, education, health status and geography. We used thematic analysis to iteratively develop themes and subthemes inductively. Results Three key themes were developed: (1) perceived general risks of health data sharing, including concerns about the limits of anonymisation, the sensitivity and scope of data requested, data governance and security, and trust in different data custodians. Participants viewed anonymisation as essential but fallible, especially for rare conditions or large linked datasets, and held a pragmatic view on sharing data with commercial organisations; (2) individual risk-benefit assessment, reflecting how people weighed potential personal harms, such as discrimination, data misuse and risks for children, against anticipated benefits, including altruism, improved care and the perceived clinical value of AI; (3) informed consent as a foundation for trust, encompassing preferences for clear, study-specific, tailored information about data use and AI purposes, and for consent processes that provided choice, avoided emotional pressure and allowed time for reflection or later withdrawal. Conclusion Trust in health-data sharing for AI is conditional and shaped by participant-level and study-specific risks and benefits. These findings highlight public expectation for transparent governance, clear justification for data use and public benefit, particularly where commercial involvement is proposed. In the context of expanding healthcare digital infrastructure and emerging UK/European Union regulatory frameworks for AI governance and reporting, understanding these expectations will be essential to building and sustaining the social licence required for large-scale data use, supporting equitable participation and representation in AI research.

title: Generative artificial intelligence adoption and the future of the primary care profession: an online survey of UK general practitioners experiences and opinions
abstract: Objective Use of large language model-based systems in healthcare has expanded rapidly since late 2022. Building on previous national surveys, we examined current generative AI (GenAI) use among UK general practitioners (GPs) and how GPs conceptualise artificial intelligence (AI), its clinical role and implications for professional practice. Methods and analysis We analysed data from the 2026 wave of the Generative AI in UK General Practice (GPAI-UK) survey is an annual, convenience sample online survey of UK GPs administered via Doctors.net.uk within a scheduled monthly omnibus targeting approximately 1000 responses. The questionnaire retained core items on GenAI use and added items on conceptualisations of AI, anticipated effects on skills and meaningfulness of work, perceived patient responses, career advice and long-term professional expectations. Descriptive statistics were used to analyse responses. Results A total of 1004 GPs completed the online survey. Just over half reported using GenAI in clinical practice (52%, 522/1004), most commonly ChatGPT, Heidi Health and Microsoft Copilot. Among users, 70% (363/522) reported that GenAI had reduced their work burden. Nearly half conceptualised GenAI as a collaborative technology working alongside clinicians (46%, 462/1004), while around one-fifth viewed it as a simple tool (21%, 209/1004) and 1 in 10 as a potential competitor (10%, 103/1004). Most expected GenAI to play at least a moderate role in routine practice within 5 years (69%, 693/1004). Looking ahead 10 years, one-third expected GenAI to change which GP skills matter most (34%, 337/1004), and 16% (163/1004) anticipated replacement of some core skills, most often documentation (811/1004), knowledge recall (509/1004) and diagnostic reasoning (442/1004). Many GPs said they would continue to encourage a career in general practice in the context of developments in AI tools; almost half had reservations (48%, 478/1004), nearly, one-third were not able to advise either way (32%, 317/1004). Most expected GenAI to substantially reshape the GP role while leaving GPs central to care (59%, 590/1004). Conclusion In this survey, over half of UK GP respondents used GenAI and primarily viewed it as a collaborative technology. GPs anticipated reconfiguration of skills and roles rather than widespread professional displacement. Understanding clinicians’ conceptualisations alongside adoption patterns is important for workforce planning, training and regulation.

title: Evaluating an LLM-assisted workflow for clinical documentation: A pilot randomized controlled trial on time and quality
abstract: by Tomohiro Takayama, Keina Sado, Kenji Suda, Hiroshi Tamura, Naoko Ueda-Arakawa, Kenji Ishihara, Yuta Ueda, Kazuya Okamoto, Luciano Henrique de Oliveira Santos, Tetsuro Oshika, Tomohiro Kuroda, Akitaka Tsujikawa, Masahiro Miyake Large language models (LLMs) have been investigated for clinical documentation, with concerns about hallucinations and factual errors. Clinician review and revision of LLM-generated drafts are considered essential; however, the impact of such a workflow on both documentation time and quality remains unknown. This single-center, parallel-group, prospective, randomized, open-label, blinded-endpoint (PROBE) pilot trial evaluated whether a clinician-in-the-loop workflow improves clinical documentation time and quality compared with clinician-only drafting. From February 18 to March 14, 2025, at the Department of Ophthalmology, Kyoto University Hospital, 21 physicians were randomized, and 17 completed the intervention. Participants were randomized to either the Clinician-in-the-loop group or the Clinician-only group. Participants created discharge summaries and referrals for six simulated patient records. The Clinician-in-the-loop group reviewed and edited LLM-generated drafts, whereas the Clinician-only group drafted documents from scratch using matched templates. Unedited LLM drafts formed the LLM-only group. Seventeen physicians submitted 48 discharge summaries and 48 discharge referrals in the Clinician-in-the-loop group, 54 of each document type in the Clinician-only group, and 48 of each in the LLM-only group. Clinician-in-the-loop showed a shorter creation time for summaries (β = −59.4 seconds; 95% CI, −150.6 to 31.7; P = .18) and a longer creation time for referrals (β = 52.9 seconds; 95% CI, −7.0 to 112.9; P = .08) than Clinician-only, although neither difference was statistically significant. In most expert-rated quality domains, the clinician-in-the-loop workflow outperformed clinician-only drafting. LLM-only drafts were fastest but had the lowest quality. In conclusion, a clinician-in-the-loop approach generally improved document quality and, although the primary analysis showed no statistically significant difference in documentation time, suggested potential time savings for certain document types. These findings highlight the importance of active clinician supervision and support further evaluation of clinician-in-the-loop workflows in real-world clinical settings. title: An LLM-based decision aid for collaborative decision-making in juvenile idiopathic arthritis: A multimethod evaluation
abstract: by Antonia Barbaric, Susanne M. Benseler, Chitra Lalloo, Xinyi Celine Liu, Alex Mariakakis, Quynh Pham, Sebastiaan J. Vastert, Rae S. M. Yeung, Joseph A. Cafazzo, Joost F. Swart Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common pediatric chronic inflammatory rheumatic condition, with substantial quality-of-life impacts. Treatment selection is complex due to limited guideline evidence, and difficult trade-offs. Decisions are often solely physician driven. We evaluated the feasibility of Large Language Model-based Decision Aid (LLM-DA) designed to support collaborative rather than solely physician decision-making in JIA care. A multi-method feasibility study was conducted in accordance with the TRIPOD-LLM checklist. The aims were twofold: first, to assess the quality of the LLM-DA (OpenAI’s o3 model) based on evaluations from three pediatric rheumatologists and an exploratory assessment by an LLM-as-a-Judge (OpenAI’s GPT-5 model); and second, to characterize perceived value of the tool from the patient perspective through a mixed methods evaluation (n = 34). For 10 de-identified use cases, rheumatologists and LLM-Judge generated treatment recommendations and scored the LLM-DA outputs on safety, factual consistency, treatment appropriateness, and preference acknowledgment. Rheumatologists rated 97% of outputs as acceptable for safety and preference acknowledgment, 60% for factual consistency, 70% for appropriateness. Treatment recommendation agreement among all evaluators and real-world data was low at almost perfect for safety and preference acknowledgement, moderate for treatment appropriateness, and poor for factual consistency, and remained the same or improved with LLM-as-a-Judge. Variability in evaluator scoring and treatment recommendations may reflect the inherent heterogeneity in acceptable JIA treatment pathways and potential limitations in the LLM-DA’s decision-making logic. Five patient themes were identified: the tool complements rheumatologist expertise, prepares patients through reflection and actionable information, builds confidence for self-advocacy, has variable value depending on the patient-physician relationship, and has potential for broader JIA self-management. These exploratory findings provide a proof-of-concept for using AI to support collaborative decision-making, while highlighting the need for future studies to determine whether LLMs can reliably support clinical practice.

title: Transparency, accountability, and scholarly integrity: A systematic narrative review of artificial intelligence governance frameworks in healthcare publication
abstract: by Amina Silva, Bruna Canever, Monica Lino, Vanessa Silva e Silva The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare research and scholarly publication has produced a rapidly expanding but fragmented ecosystem of reporting guidelines, governance frameworks, editorial policies, and regulatory instruments, imposing significant burdens on researchers, reviewers, and editors. This systematic narrative review identified, stratified, and synthesized governance frameworks and reporting standards addressing transparent and ethical AI use in healthcare publications, and characterized the governance trajectory from predictive model standards to generative AI oversight. Fourteen Boolean search strings were executed in PubMed (MEDLINE) covering 1 January 2018–19 May 2026, supplemented by manual searching of the EQUATOR Network guideline library. Records were deduplicated and prioritized using a relevance-scoring algorithm. Of 30,276 deduplicated records, 888 progressed to human screening; 100 publications were included, comprising 69 governance instruments and policies classified across four evidence tiers and 31 contextual evidence sources. Included sources spanned six thematic groups: predictive and diagnostic AI frameworks (G1); sociotechnical and lifecycle governance (G2); generative AI and LLM-specific standards (G3); specialty-specific extensions (G4); surgical reporting updates (G5); and editorial and publication policy (G6). Analysis identified four consecutive phases of governance development from 2018 to 2026, characterized by a shift from model performance transparency toward comprehensive sociotechnical accountability. Three governance tensions emerged: the trade-off between framework specificity and universal applicability; the gap between disclosure-focused standards and lifecycle governance; and the risk of epistemic conflation, whereby heterogeneous instruments are perceived as carrying equivalent authority when treated as interchangeable. AI governance in healthcare publications remains fragmented and epistemically uneven. Advancing the field requires harmonization across evidence tiers, adaptive updating mechanisms, and lifecycle-oriented governance frameworks.

title: Prevalent knowledge omissions: An unseen risk of LLMs in patient-friendly adaptation of medical literature
abstract: by Mei Chen, Shibin Wang Large language models (LLMs) can produce patient-friendly adaptations, such as simplifying specialized medical literature for readers with a middle school education. However, any distortion of knowledge during this process may have serious consequences. Current evaluations overlook such risks. In this study, we proposes a knowledge triplet comparison (KTC) method to assess knowledge distortion by systematically quantifying the retention and alteration of medical knowledge before and after text adaptation. Using the Chemical-Disease Relations dataset, this study evaluates the performance of six LLMs across eight adaptation scenarios (e.g., adjusting reading level, modifying text length) and draws the following key conclusions: First, from a quantitative perspective, knowledge distortion is prevalent in all adaptation scenarios, with the models retaining only approximately half of the original medical knowledge. Additionally, about 10% more knowledge is added. Second, the distribution of knowledge distortion follows a clear categorical distribution pattern, with etiology and pathological mechanisms, as well as complications and risk factors, being the most frequently distortion types. Third, targeted corrections through prompt engineering have no significant impact on the quantity and categorical distribution patterns of knowledge distortion, indicating that knowledge distortion is persistent and regular. This study shows that, in addition to the more obvious risk of hallucinations caused by a small amount of added knowledge, patient-friendly rewrites by LLMs also pose a significant risk of subtle yet potentially serious knowledge omissions. Furthermore, this research reveals the regularity of knowledge distortion, laying the groundwork for further investigation into the patterns of knowledge distortion and the development of solutions to this problem.

title: The world’s oldest living culture leads the way with interpretable generative AI: Aboriginal women shaping the future of perinatal mental health services
abstract: by Guanjin Wang, Hachem Bennamoun, Wai Hang Kwok, Rehan Raza, Ferdous Sohel, Bridgette Kelly, Trish Ratajczak, Corinne Reid, Rhonda Marriott, Roz Walker, Jayne Kotz, Tracy Reibel Despite their strengths, Aboriginal mothers experience significant health disparities, including perinatal mental health challenges influenced by social, historical, and cultural determinants. Routine risk screening informs follow-up care, yet conventional approaches often fail to address cultural considerations. The Baby Coming You Ready (BCYR) program provides a strengths-based, culturally adapted digital assessment designed to enhance perinatal mental health care. However, some clinicians continue to rely primarily on conventional risk scores, which can neglect broader contextual circumstances influencing Aboriginal mothers, including cultural strengths and protective factors, thereby limiting the program’s full impact. This exploratory model-development study examined whether generative AI data augmentation combined with an intrinsically interpretable machine-learning model could support culturally contextualised prediction of perinatal psychological distress among Aboriginal mothers. We analysed deidentified BCYR pilot data from 293 Aboriginal mothers across six Western Australian sites. After excluding five records with incomplete outcome data, the analytic dataset included 288 participants. Models were evaluated using repeated internal train-test splits, with synthetic data used only for training augmentation and performance assessed on held-out real test data. The highest internal performance was observed for the TVAE-augmented Explainable Boosting Machine at an augmentation ratio of 1.0, with an accuracy of 0.867, an F1 score of 0.817, and an AUC of 0.934. Model explanations identified self-blame, loneliness, family pride, day-to-day management, sleep, and related contextual factors as influential contributors to model-estimated risk. These explanations are intended as prompts for culturally safe discussion and clinical reflection. Findings suggest that interpretable generative AI may have potential to support culturally responsive perinatal mental health assessment. However, broader community-governed external validation and prospective clinical workflow evaluation are required before clinical implementation.

title: Performance of large language models in the Chinese National Medical Licensing Examinations and Beyond: Scoping review
abstract: by Hui Zong, Jiao Wang, Jiaxue Cha, Rongrong Wu, Shanshan Hu, Yan Zhao, Bairong Shen Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 and DeepSeek have shown potential in medical education and assessment. In China, the Chinese National Medical Licensing Examination (CNMLE) has become a critical benchmark for evaluating LLMs’ professional knowledge and reasoning ability in non-English contexts. This scoping review aims to synthesize research evaluating LLM performance on the CNMLE and related Chinese medical examinations, identifying performance trends, methodological gaps, and future directions. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed and Web of Science were searched on June 12, 2025, using terms related to LLMs and Chinese medical examinations. Studies were included if they evaluated any LLM on national-level Chinese medical exams and reported performance metrics. Two reviewers screened and extracted data. Study quality was assessed using a 12-item checklist covering dataset characteristics, LLM setup, and evaluation methods. Fisher’s exact test was used to assess differences in the passing rates of different LLMs. 14 studies were included, covering 51 evaluation records across 8 types of Chinese medical examinations, including CNMLE and specialty exams such as critical care, radiation oncology, and ultrasound medicine. Exam years ranged from 2017 to 2024, with a shift toward using recent exams. A total of 9 LLMs were evaluated, including GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o, ERNIE, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-72B, Baichuan2-7B, Baichuan2-13B and DISC-MedLLM. GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 achieved the highest scores of 552 (92.00%) and 523 (87.20%) in the 2024 CNMLE, respectively, both surpassing the passing threshold. In an exploratory comparison, GPT-4 achieved a higher pass rate than GPT-3.5 with a statistically significant difference, although inconsistencies in datasets, model transparency, and evaluation criteria persist across the included studies. LLMs show improving performance on Chinese medical exams, especially newer models. Nevertheless, future research should prioritize standardized benchmarks, multimodal capabilities, and transparent evaluation to ensure meaningful clinical relevance and educational value.

title: Retrieval-to-abstraction LLM-assisted literature synthesis: Case demonstrations in digital health technology-enabled randomized controlled trial outcome reporting
abstract: by Taylor B. Harrison, Dian Hu, Heling Jia, Shyang Hong Tan, Fang Chen, Zhongyu Zhang, Qiuhao Lu, Jinlian Wang, Liwei Wang, Ming Huang, Larry J. Prokop, Matt Hoy, Jennifer St. Sauver, Sunyang Fu, Hongfang Liu Systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) support evidence-based clinical advancement. Clinical trial reporting guidelines, including CONSORT, establish common data elements that support systematic synthesis of published trial outcomes. However, the rapid rise of digital health technologies presents new challenges for reporting guidelines, and substantial real-world reporting heterogeneity has been observed. Therefore, machine-assisted evaluation of reporting adherence offers a pathway for more agile information management to accommodate the diverse and disruptive nature of digital health technology-enabled RCTs. Here, we propose an accelerated retrieval-to-abstraction literature synthesis framework to conduct article screening, text and table data preprocessing, and full-text review using an unmodified pretrained large language model. We apply this methodology in two digital health technology-enabled RCT case studies evaluating adherence to technology and digital health equity guideline reporting items. Large language model performance was on par with inter-annotator agreement F1 scores (≥0.9) in both screening and information-extraction tasks. These findings support the scalability and rigor of accelerated evidence synthesis and demonstrate the importance of common reporting elements across digital health technology-enabled RCTs.

title: Recent advances in multimodal deep learning for breast cancer diagnosis using data fusion vision language models and foundation models
abstract: Breast cancer remains one of the most prevalent cancers worldwide, underscoring the need for reliable diagnostic approaches that can support accurate and timely clinical assessment. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning, have enabled the development of multimodal systems that integrate complementary data sources, including medical images, radiology reports, clinical information, and genomic data. Such approaches aim to exploit information that may not be fully captured by a single modality and have shown promising performance in breast cancer diagnosis and related prediction tasks. This review provides a comprehensive and critical overview of multimodal deep learning approaches for breast cancer diagnosis published between January 2021 and September 2026. It examines the principal data modalities used in multimodal systems, including mammography, ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, histopathology, radiology reports, clinical information, and genomic data. The review also analyzes major multimodal fusion strategies and traces the evolution of the field from conventional machine-learning and radiomics-based approaches to deep learning architectures, vision-language models, and foundation models. Recent multimodal models are discussed according to the data modalities employed, model architectures, fusion strategies, clinical or diagnostic tasks, datasets, and reported performance. Particular attention is given to approaches integrating medical imaging with radiology reports and other textual information, including emerging vision-language and foundation-model-based methods for breast imaging. Publicly available datasets and multimodal resources used in breast cancer research are also summarized and compared. Despite recent progress, important challenges remain, including the limited availability of large-scale multimodal datasets, restricted access to paired image–report datasets, missing modalities, limited external validation, uncertainty estimation, explainability, fairness, generalizability, and barriers to clinical workflow integration. Current evidence is still predominantly retrospective and technical; therefore, reported improvements in model performance should not be interpreted as demonstrated clinical benefit without prospective validation. Future research should focus on robust multimodal foundation models, explainable and trustworthy artificial intelligence, federated and privacy-preserving learning, standardized external validation, and prospective clinical evaluation. Overall, this review provides an updated synthesis of methodological developments, multimodal data integration strategies, emerging vision-language and foundation models, and translational challenges in multimodal artificial intelligence for breast cancer diagnosis.

title: Integrating extended reality into preoperative neurosurgical planning: exploratory evaluation of planning-related behavior in an instrumented hybrid framework
abstract: BackgroundExtended reality (XR) has increasingly been investigated for visualization and preoperative planning in neurosurgery. However, evaluation has often focused on visualization, usability, technical performance, and task outcomes, while comparatively less attention has been given to quantifying observable planning-related behavior.MethodsWe developed and evaluated an instrumented hybrid desktop–XR framework integrating conventional image-based planning with immersive exploration of patient-specific neurosurgical anatomy. The framework synchronized selected visualization and interaction states between a 3D Slicer-based desktop environment and an XR workspace and captured spatial, anatomical, workflow, interaction, and subjective measures. Twenty participants with different levels of clinical experience evaluated two patient-specific tumor cases.ResultsAll participants completed both evaluation cases without session-ending technical interruption. Entry–tumor-center directions showed substantial convergence, with directional convergence of 0.881 for the GBM case and 0.965 for the LGG case, while anatomical structure selection showed fair overall agreement (Fleiss’ κ=0.397). Workflow, interaction, and subjective measures provided complementary information on task execution and user experience.ConclusionThe instrumented hybrid desktop–XR framework demonstrated technical and procedural feasibility under the study conditions for capturing complementary quantitative measures of spatial planning, anatomical selection, workflow, interaction, and subjective experience. These findings demonstrate that selected components of preoperative planning can be made observable and quantifiable within an XR-supported workflow. The measures should currently be regarded as descriptive behavioral measures rather than validated indicators of planning quality, expertise, or clinical correctness. The framework provides a methodological basis for subsequent validation using larger cohorts, more diverse cases, conventional-workflow comparisons, and expert or clinical reference criteria.
authors: Anna Drechslerová, Georg Widhalm, Gilbert Hangel, et al.

title: From principles to practice: operationalizing responsible AI governance across predictive and generative clinical AI
abstract: Responsible artificial intelligence (AI) governance in healthcare is increasingly supported by international principles addressing transparency, accountability, safety, explainability, and lifecycle risk management. Yet a persistent implementation gap remains between these institution-level principles and the concrete controls encountered when an AI service is used in clinical practice. This Perspective argues that responsible AI should be operationalized at the functional points where clinical AI outputs are produced, explained, and communicated. We use three functional domains—Capability, Explainability, and Communication—as an organizing structure for translating existing governance principles into application-level specifications. The approach accommodates both predictive AI (PAI) and generative AI (GAI) while recognizing their different risk profiles. For PAI, governance emphasizes target and prediction-horizon definition, calibration, thresholds, drift, external validation, and alert burden. For GAI, it emphasizes task boundaries, source traceability, hallucination control, version management, human verification, and constraints on write-back or autonomous action. Two dialysis-related applications illustrate how the same governance vocabulary can be instantiated differently across AI modalities. Operationalizing responsible AI in this way does not introduce new governance principles; rather, it organizes existing requirements into observable, reviewable, and auditable controls embedded in clinical AI services and workflows.
authors: Chung-Feng Liu, Chia-Jung Chen, Yen-Ling Ko

title: Artificial intelligence in odontology education
abstract: IntroductionArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in dental education as a tool to support teaching, learning, assessment, and clinical decision-making. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on the implementation and educational impact of AI technologies in undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing dental education.MethodologyA PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted using Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 evaluating AI applications in dental education were identified using predefined PICO criteria. Educational outcomes included knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, procedural skills, learner engagement, and perceptions of AI-assisted learning.ResultsThe included literature reflects an expansion from machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision systems primarily evaluated for diagnostic support toward generative AI platforms, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Across the included studies, AI applications were frequently associated with favorable diagnostic and examination performance and, in selected educational contexts, with supportive findings related to clinical reasoning, technical competency, feedback, and self-directed learning. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical performance assessments and observational or cross-sectional designs.DiscussionAI is increasingly being explored as a potential complementary educational resource, with applications including interactive tutoring, adaptive learning, and support for clinical reasoning. Nevertheless, heterogeneous methodologies and limited longitudinal evidence indicate the need for standardized educational evaluation and responsible curricular integration.ConclusionAI shows potential as a complementary resource in dental education. Its integration should remain pedagogically guided and ethically supervised while future research establishes its educational effectiveness through standardized and longitudinal evaluation.

title: Real-Time Influenza Surveillance Using DeepSeek-Augmented BERT Classification on Chinese Social Media: Infodemiology Study
abstract: Background: Traditional influenza surveillance systems rely on sentinel hospitals and often experience a 1‐ to 2-week reporting lag, limiting timely public health response. Social media platforms provide real-time data streams, but extracting reliable epidemiological signals remains challenging due to substantial linguistic noise. Although large language models (LLMs) improve semantic extraction, their computational cost limits routine deployment in resource-constrained public health settings. Objective: This study proposes and evaluates a hybrid framework that distills knowledge from an LLM (DeepSeek) into a lightweight bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)–based classifier for real-time influenza surveillance using Weibo data from Guangdong Province, China, during the 2025 influenza season. The study further assesses the temporal alignment between the derived signal and official influenza-like illness (ILI) surveillance data. Methods: A total of 389,959 Weibo posts from epidemiological weeks 7 to 50 (February 10 to December 14, 2025) were collected using a domain-specific keyword strategy. After multistage filtering, 99,158 posts were retained for analysis. A DeepSeek-Chat model was used to generate pseudo-labels for 2500 posts via zero-shot prompting, which were evaluated against expert annotations (Cohen κ=0.846) and used to fine-tune a Chinese-RoBERTa-WWM-ext classifier (a robustly optimized BERT pretraining approach). A chronological train-validation-test split was applied to reduce temporal leakage. The trained model was used to construct a weekly Weibo Flu Index. This index was compared with keyword-based and Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) + logistic regression baselines using time-lag Pearson correlation (0‐5 wk) against official ILI% data. Savitzky-Golay smoothing and second-derivative analysis were applied to identify epidemic inflection points and peak timing. Results: The classifier achieved an accuracy of 85.1% and an -score of 0.800 on a chronologically held-out test set, identifying 29,779 posts (30.0%) as ILI self-reports among 99,158 posts. The BERT-derived index showed the strongest correlation with official ILI% at lag 0 (=0.523, 95% CI 0.268‐0.710; ²=0.274) and lag 1 (=0.446, 95% CI 0.169‐0.658), compared with the keyword baseline (lag 0: =0.481, ²=0.231) and TF-IDF baseline (lag 0: =0.185, =0.034). Inflection analysis indicated that the Weibo-derived signal preceded both the epidemic rise (week 44 vs week 45) and peak (week 48 vs week 49) in official ILI data, corresponding to an approximate 1-week lead at both transition points. Conclusions: The results suggest that a DeepSeek-augmented lightweight BERT classifier can extract meaningful influenza-related signals from noisy Chinese social media data and produce a surveillance index that shows an approximate 1-week lead relative to official ILI reporting, with improved performance over keyword-based and TF-IDF approaches. This framework provides a proof-of-concept for cost-effective real-time influenza nowcasting using social media data.

title: Evaluating the Performance of Five Leading Large Language Models in Generating Health Education Materials for Patients With Infertility: Comparative Analysis
abstract: Background: Patients with infertility often have inadequate reproductive health literacy (RHL), while existing health education materials may be difficult to read, overly complex, and insufficiently tailored to individual needs. In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have created new opportunities to improve health education through their ability to generate and interpret medical information. However, their applicability and content quality in infertility education remain insufficiently evaluated. Objective: This study systematically evaluated the readability and content quality of LLM-generated health education materials for patients with infertility, identified model strengths and limitations, and provided evidence to support their standardized use in reproductive health. Methods: This study selected DeepSeek-R1, ChatGPT (GPT-5.2 Plus), Kimi 2.5, Qwen 3, and Gemini 3 as the study subjects. Based on the theoretical framework of RHL, this study developed a standardized question list comprising 6 dimensions and 93 items, and used unified prompts to generate health education texts in both Chinese and English. In this study, the Datayze Readability Analyzer was used to assess readability via the Flesch Reading Ease, Gunning Fog Index, and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Meanwhile, the content quality was evaluated in a double-blinded manner by reproductive medicine experts across 3 dimensions: accuracy, comprehensiveness, and humanistic care. Repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to compare performance across the LLMs, and Pearson correlation analysis was conducted to examine the associations between readability and content quality. A radar chart was used to evaluate the overall performance of each model. Results: The 5 LLMs differed significantly in both text readability and content quality. In terms of readability, Gemini 3 and Qwen 3 performed best, with significantly higher FRE scores than the other 3 models. DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi 2.5 performed least favorably, with FKGL scores corresponding to a ninth-grade reading level. ChatGPT (GPT-5.2 Plus) showed intermediate performance. In terms of content quality, Kimi 2.5 performed best across accuracy, comprehensiveness, and humanistic care, followed by DeepSeek-R1. ChatGPT (GPT-5.2 Plus) performed least favorably. Analysis revealed significant negative correlations between readability and content comprehensiveness for texts generated by Kimi 2.5, indicating a trade-off between these 2 attributes. The composite radar chart analysis showed that Kimi 2.5 achieved the highest score (11,594.33), whereas ChatGPT (GPT-5.2 Plus) had the lowest score (5555.83). Conclusions: Different LLMs showed significant differences in performance in generating health education texts for patients with infertility. In some models, readability was negatively correlated with content comprehensiveness. Under the conditions of this study, Kimi 2.5 demonstrated strong overall performance. However, no model achieved the best performance across all evaluation dimensions. Future applications of LLMs in reproductive health education will require domain-specific optimization, context-specific adaptation, and systematic quality control to support more accurate, comprehensive, and patient-centered communication.

title: Effects of Temporal Information Structure on Causal Explanations Generated by Large Language Models: Experimental Study Using Lung Cancer Incidence Data
abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to causal explanation in public health and epidemiology. However, recent studies suggest that LLMs exhibit instability in processing temporal information, which raises concerns about their suitability for generating coherent causal explanations. Despite this, little is known about how distinct components of temporal information influence LLM-generated causal explanations in epidemiological contexts. Objective: This study aimed to examine how event ordering and the validity and presence of explicit temporal information affect LLM-generated causal explanations of long-term lung cancer incidence trends. Specifically, we evaluated their effects on evidence grounding, causal alignment, and disease specificity. Methods: We used a 2×3 factorial design manipulating event ordering (chronological vs randomized) and explicit temporal information (accurate, inaccurate, or absent). Five LLMs (GPT-5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.8, Qwen3-32B, and Llama 3.3 70B Instruct) generated 600 causal explanations of long-term lung cancer incidence trends using Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) data and PubMed-derived event statements. The effects of ordering and information were assessed using regression and factorial ANOVA. Results: Randomized ordering showed higher evidence grounding than chronological ordering (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.53, 95% CI 1.89-3.37; P Conclusions: More accurate or structured temporal information did not necessarily improve LLM-generated causal explanations. Randomized ordering was associated with greater evidence utilization, whereas chronological ordering supported causal alignment across all information conditions, particularly for decreasing trajectories. These findings suggest that temporal context should be structured not only to provide temporal information but also to support the intended characteristics of the resulting explanation.
authors: Eunzi Jeong, Wonjeong Jeong, Kyoung Hee Oh, et al.

title: Generative Large Language Models for Psychiatric Concept Detection in Spanish-Language Electronic Health Records: Development and Evaluation Study
abstract: Background: The accurate detection of clinical symptoms in electronic health records (EHRs) is pivotal for advancing large-scale genetic and longitudinal studies in psychiatry. Free-text clinical notes are an essential source of symptom-level information, particularly in psychiatry; however, the automated extraction of symptoms from clinical text remains challenging. Objective: We aimed to evaluate the ability of open-source generative large language models (LLMs) to detect psychiatric symptom-level concepts from clinical text in Spanish and to develop a new fine-tuned, open-source LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information. Methods: We tested 11 open-source generative LLMs for their ability to detect 109 psychiatric concepts from clinical text, using annotated EHR notes from a psychiatric hospital in Colombia. The LLMs were evaluated both “out-of-the-box” and after fine-tuning and compared against a traditional natural language processing (tNLP) method developed from the same data. To develop a fine-tuned LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information, we created a novel synthetic dataset, leveraging real concept annotations while generating fully synthetic clinical text, and fine-tuned a top-performing LLM on these data. Fine-tuned model generalizability was assessed through cross-site evaluation using data from a second independent hospital in Colombia. Results: We show that while base LLM performance was poor to moderate (zero-shot: 0.2-0.6 macro- F 1 ; few-shot: 0.2-0.74 macro- F 1 ), it improved significantly after fine-tuning (0.75-0.86 macro- F 1 ), with several fine-tuned LLMs outperforming the tNLP method. In total, 100 psychiatric concepts could be reliably detected ( F 1 >0.8) using either a fine-tuned LLM or tNLP. Using the synthetic dataset, we developed Mistral-small-psych, a new LLM capable of detecting psychiatric concepts from Spanish clinical text with performance comparable to models trained on real EHR data (macro- F 1 =0.79) while remaining fully distributable. In cross-site evaluations, most LLMs generalized well, with small out-of-domain performance losses (macro- F 1 decrease of 0.02-0.16). Conclusions: This work provides the first large-scale, cross-institutional evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs for psychiatric concept detection in Spanish EHRs, introduces a privacy-preserving pathway for building shareable clinical natural language processing models, and presents a new open model for extracting symptom-level psychiatric information from Spanish clinical text.

title: Emotional and Literacy Adaptation in Large Language Model–Based Medical Guidance: Development and Usability Study
abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as conversational agents for communication and guidance, but their ability to adapt responses to a patient’s emotional state and literacy level remains insufficiently characterized. In patient-facing scenarios, effective communication requires not only accurate medical content but also appropriate tone, clarity, and responsiveness to user vulnerability. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate, within a controlled, single-scenario experimental design, the ability of contemporary LLMs to adapt medical guidance responses to different levels of emotional sensitivity and literacy, and to assess their consistency in both generating and interpreting such adaptations. Methods: A controlled benchmark was designed to evaluate how 4 LLMs adapt medical guidance responses to predefined emotional and literacy levels for a realistic patient profile asking an open-ended question. To establish a robust performance baseline, one model was deployed locally (Gemma 3 27B), and 3 are cloud-based (Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT 5.2). Each model was tested across all combinations of 5 emotional levels, 3 literacy levels, and 3 prompt-verbosity variants, yielding 45 responses per model. Generated responses were assessed against human-reviewed ground truth for emotional and literacy alignment. A separate self-evaluation procedure measured each model’s ability to interpret its own outputs using the same adaptation framework. The study also examined generation-interpretation consistency and quantitative text properties, with particular attention to response length and verbosity. Results: Literacy adaptation was consistently accurate across models, often achieving near-zero error, indicating strong capability in adjusting explanatory complexity. In contrast, emotional adaptation showed greater variability and was more sensitive to model architecture and prompt design. The larger cloud-based models demonstrated more stable performance overall, while the local model exhibited higher variability, particularly under shorter prompts. A systematic asymmetry was observed between generation and interpretation. The models frequently misclassified low emotional and literacy levels as “normal,” suggesting limitations in recognizing user needs. Quantitative analysis revealed that response length increased with both emotional sensitivity and literacy level, with prompt verbosity and model-specific tendencies acting as secondary factors. Conclusions: Within our scenario, current LLMs demonstrated the capacity to support adaptive medical guidance, but their performance was uneven across dimensions, especially in terms of emotional generation and interpretation. For health care applications, these systems should be treated as assistive tools under human oversight rather than as autonomous communicators, with careful consideration of ethical, privacy, and safety implications in sensitive health contexts. title: Estimating Functional Independence Measure Scores From Japanese Rehabilitation Notes Using a Large Language Model: Retrospective Study
abstract: Background: The Functional Independence Measure (FIM) is a standard functional assessment tool in rehabilitation medicine; however, formal assessments are often conducted only at limited intervals. Free-text clinical notes contain more frequent observations of patients’ functional status and may complement these assessments. Objective: This study aimed to estimate item-level FIM scores from Japanese free-text rehabilitation notes using a locally deployed large language model (LLM) and to evaluate estimation performance; item-level estimability; and differences across diseases, therapy types, and admission FIM severity groups. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed free-text notes from physical therapy (PT), occupational therapy (OT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) for patients hospitalized with cerebral infarction (CeI), hip fracture (HF), or vertebral fracture (VBF) at Saiseikai Moriyama Municipal Hospital between October 2019 and September 2024. Using zero-shot prompting, an LLM estimated all FIM items from each note. Estimated scores were matched to reference FIM scores recorded for the same patient on the same calendar date. Performance was evaluated using the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error, and quadratic weighted kappa. Estimation rates and comparisons with modal-score and last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) baselines were also examined. Results: Among 2,952,702 eligible note-item pairs from 164,039 retained rehabilitation-note-level outputs, the model produced 980,000 valid estimates, corresponding to an overall estimation rate of 33.2%. Among 170,744 note-item opportunities with an available same-day reference score, 57,246 (33.5%) were estimable, of which 77.7% (44,481/57,246) were within 1 point of the reference score. Estimates derived from OT notes had a lower MAE than those derived from PT notes in CeI and HF, whereas the difference was not significant in VBF. The LLM outperformed the modal-score baseline but had a higher MAE than the LOCF overall (0.825 vs 0.648). Conclusions: The locally deployed LLM shows the potential to derive item-level FIM estimates from Japanese rehabilitation notes. Among estimable note-item pairs with a same-day reference FIM score, 77.7% were within 1 point of the reference score. These findings support the potential use of LLM-based estimation to structure functional information contained in routine rehabilitation notes and complement periodic FIM assessments. Further integration of multidisciplinary clinical records and external validation are needed to improve estimability and evaluate its value for longitudinal functional monitoring.

title: Evaluating Internet-Based AI Chatbots as Unregulated Digital Health Resources in Dental Emergency Management: Comparative Multilingual Study
abstract: Background: Publicly accessible, internet-based AI chatbots have emerged as unregulated digital health resources that clinicians and patients consult in real time, including during acute medical emergencies. In dental practice—where life-threatening events such as anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, and severe hypoglycemia can unfold within seconds—the unsupervised use of these tools as point-of-care decision aids poses uncharacterized patient safety risks. Despite widespread deployment, no study has systematically evaluated the accuracy, temporal consistency, or multilingual reliability of contemporary large language model (LLM)–based chatbots specifically for dental medical emergency management. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy, temporal stability, and multilingual performance of five contemporary LLM-based chatbots when queried on the management of medical emergencies in dental practice. Methods: A comparative study was conducted to assess five AI chatbots: ChatGPT-5.2 (OpenAI), Gemini 3.1 (Google), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek AI), Grok 4.20 (xAI), and Kimi K2.5 (Moonshot AI). A total of 130 questions covering dental medical emergency management were developed and categorized into four formats: multiple-choice questions (MCQs), yes-or-no questions, open-ended WH questions, and clinical scenario questions. Each question was presented using two prompting strategies (basic and advanced) across three languages (English, Arabic, and Chinese). Data collection was performed over seven consecutive days, generating 27,300 chatbot responses. Responses were evaluated by language-specific expert reviewers and classified as correct or incorrect based on established clinical references. Statistical analysis was performed using chi-square tests to assess associations between accuracy and study variables. Pairwise post hoc comparisons of column proportions were conducted using z-tests with Bonferroni correction. Results: A total of 27,300 responses were analyzed; 25,377 (92.96%) were correct. Question type significantly influenced chatbot performance (<.001), with MCQs demonstrating the highest accuracy (5942/6300, 94.3%), and WH questions demonstrating the lowest accuracy (7686/8400, 91.5%). Language also showed a significant association with accuracy (=.01), with English prompts achieving the highest accuracy (8512/9100, 93.5%). Chatbot model performance differed significantly (<.001), with Gemini 3.1 demonstrating the highest accuracy (5176/5460, 94.8%; 95% CI 94.21%‐95.39%), followed by ChatGPT-5.2 (5105/5460, 93.5%; 95% CI 92.85%‐94.15%) and Kimi K2.5 (5071/5460, 92.9%). Prompt complexity and testing day did not significantly affect response accuracy (=.69 and =.96, respectively). Conclusions: Current LLM-based chatbots demonstrate high accuracy in answering structured questions related to dental medical emergency management. However, performance varies according to question format and language, and the presence of incorrect responses highlights potential safety concerns. AI chatbots may serve as educational tools, but their use as real-time decision support during dental medical emergencies should be approached with caution.

title: Bayesian Demonstration Selection for LLM-Based Dementia Detection From Patient-Generated Text
abstract: Detecting dementia from spontaneous speech transcripts is an important yet challenging text classification task. The linguistic cues that signal cognitive decline are often subtle, and standard in-context learning (ICL) methods struggle to select effective demonstrations. We explore Bayesian-motivated strategies for demonstration selection, using probabilistic factorization to choose better demonstrations and thereby improve Large Language Model (LLM) based dementia detection. We introduce two class-balanced selection methods. The first applies a naive Bayes (word-level) independence assumption to rank training samples within each class, then uses beam search to select diverse speech examples from both the dementia and healthy-control groups. The second method relaxes the word-level independence assumption. Rather than estimating document likelihood from independent unigram and bigram counts, it scores each candidate using an LLM-based class-contrast margin computed from token log-likelihoods under class-conditioned prefixes. It further adds an embedding-based similarity term so that selected demonstrations are encouraged to be relevant to the test transcript. We evaluate our methods using three lightweight open-source LLMs on two dementia-detection datasets. We find that both methods generally outperform prior state-of-the-art (SOTA) ICL techniques, standard retrieval baselines, and supervised systems, without introducing any new optimized prompts. These results suggest that Bayesian-guided ICL demo selection with some simplifying assumptions offers a principled way to improve ICL without supervised fine-tuning.

title: Explainable AI for Mental Disorder Detection on Social Media: A Survey and Outlook
abstract: Mental health (MH) is a complex global challenge. The widespread use of online social media (OSM) provides a rich source of data for supporting MH analytics. This article presents a comprehensive review of AI- and data-driven approaches for mental disorder detection (MDD) using OSM, with a particular focus on explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). We summarize traditional diagnostic practices and provide an integrated overview of modern deep learning models, emphasizing how their growing complexity increases the need for transparent and trustworthy explanations. We review a wide range of explainability techniques applied in this domain, including interpretable models, post-hoc attribution methods, attention- and graph-based explanations, and emerging LLM-driven approaches, and outline commonly used datasets and evaluation practices. Finally, we identify key challenges such as data limitations, bias, and the need for clinically meaningful explanations, and propose directions for future research. This survey offers a comprehensive foundation for developing explainable, reliable, and ethically informed MDD systems for social media.
authors: Yusif Ibrahimov;Tarique Anwar;Tommy Yuan;

title: RGPO: Ranking-Guided Preference Optimization for Reliable Clinical Reasoning
abstract: Medical question answering (QA) in healthcare systems requires advanced reasoning that integrates domain knowledge with clinical workflows. However, existing large language models (LLMs) often generate reasoning chains that lack factual accuracy and clinical reliability. We propose ranking-guided preference optimization (RGPO) for Reliable Clinical Reasoning, a framework that combines reinforcement learning with preference driven reasoning refinement to enhance clinical chain-of-thought performance in LLM-based healthcare systems. RGPO employs task-adaptive reasoning templates aligned with clinical protocols and a probabilistic evaluation mechanism that integrates with healthcare information systems, including electronic health records (EHRs) and clinical documentation, while automatically identifying and correcting low-quality reasoning chains. Unlike traditional pairwise preference methods, RGPO introduces groupwise ranking optimization based on the Bradley–Terry model with Kullback–Leibler (KL)-divergence regularization for stable clinical deployment. The framework addresses key challenges, including multimodal data integration, clinical validation, and real-world interoperability. Experiments on PubMedQA, MedQA-USMLE, and real-world validation at Far Eastern Memorial Hospital (FEMH) demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines. Our 2B-parameter model outperforms larger 7B–20B models, including medical-specialized variants, while maintaining computational efficiency for healthcare deployment. These results demonstrate that combining preference optimization with quality-driven refinement provides a scalable, clinically validated approach to building reliable medical LLMs for practical healthcare applications.
